posts.post_title: Genus of Newcastle disease virus (APMV-1)
posts.post_content: Newcastle disease virus (APMV-1) belongs to which genus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Avulavirus

Newcastle disease virus is classified under the genus Avulavirus.

Correct Option Explanation

It belongs to family Paramyxoviridae, subfamily Paramyxovirinae, and is designated Avian Paramyxovirus 1 (APMV-1), one of nine APMV species (APMV-1 to APMV-9).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morbillivirus includes rinderpest and canine distemper viruses, not APMV-1.
  • Pneumovirus includes avian and human respiratory syncytial-type viruses, unrelated to APMV-1.
  • Henipavirus includes Nipah and Hendra viruses, a separate paramyxovirus genus.
Know More
  • ND is caused by strains of APMV-1 only.
  • APMV-1 cross-reacts with APMV-2 and APMV-3.
  • ND virus is OIE List A, Risk Group II.
  • Synonyms include Ranikhet disease and Pseudo fowlpest.

posts.post_title: Number of APMV species under genus Avulavirus
posts.post_content: How many different species are recognised under the genus Avulavirus, numbered APMV-1 to APMV-9?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Nine

There are nine species under genus Avulavirus, numbered APMV-1 to APMV-9.

Correct Option Explanation

Strains of APMV-1 cause Newcastle disease, and APMV-1 cross-reacts serologically with APMV-2 and APMV-3.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Six, seven and eleven are simply incorrect counts and do not correspond to the documented number of APMV species.
Know More
  • ND virus surface has HN protein projections.
  • Virus size ranges 150-300 nm.
  • Contains six major structural proteins: NP, P, M, F, HN, L.
  • Also carries non-structural proteins V and W.

posts.post_title: Newcastle disease virus surface glycoprotein for attachment
posts.post_content: Which surface protein of Newcastle disease virus is responsible for attachment and release of the virus from host cells, and is also used for serologic identification?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemagglutinin-neuraminidase (HN)

The HN protein mediates viral attachment, release from host cells, and serologic identification.

Correct Option Explanation

HN is a surface projection on the envelope; antibodies against it are measured in the HI test, where a titre of log2 3 indicates protection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Matrix protein (M) lies beneath the envelope and helps in virus budding, not attachment.
  • Fusion protein (F) enables membrane fusion and is critical for pathogenesis, not primary attachment.
  • Nucleoprotein (NP) is part of the internal ribonucleoprotein complex, not a surface protein.
Know More
  • RNP complex is formed by RNA with NP, P and L proteins.
  • Virus causes agglutination of chicken and human O erythrocytes.
  • Elution occurs after about 30 minutes.
  • Preferred cultivation route is the allantoic cavity of 9-11 day eggs.

posts.post_title: Mean death time test classification of ND strains
posts.post_content: Based on the Mean Death Time (MDT) test in embryonated eggs, a Newcastle disease virus strain that kills embryos in 60 to 90 hours is classified as which pathotype?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mesogenic

Strains killing embryos in 60-90 hours by MDT are classed as mesogenic.

Correct Option Explanation

By MDT, velogenic strains kill in under 60 hours, mesogenic in 60-90 hours, and lentogenic strains take more than 90 hours.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Velogenic strains are more virulent, killing embryos faster (under 60 hours), e.g. strains Hertz 33, Texas GB.
  • Lentogenic strains are mild, e.g. La Sota, F, Ulster 2C, used as live vaccines.
  • Avirulent strain V4 is not defined by the MDT time bands used for the other three pathotypes.
Know More
  • Other pathotyping tests: ICPI and IVPI.
  • ICPI is done in day-old chicks over 8 days.
  • IVPI is done in 6-week-old SPF chickens over 10 days.
  • Molecular typing studies amino acids 112-119 of the F gene.

posts.post_title: Vaccine strain used for lentogenic ND priming vaccine
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a live lentogenic vaccine strain commonly used for priming immunization against Newcastle disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: La Sota

La Sota is a live lentogenic strain used for priming vaccination in young chicks.

Correct Option Explanation

Lentogenic vaccines (HB1, La Sota, F, V4, Ulster 2C) are given via eye or nasal drops; only La Sota may cause a mild post-vaccinal reaction.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Komarov is a mesogenic strain used as a secondary vaccine after lentogenic priming.
  • Mukteswar is also a mesogenic secondary vaccine strain, used mainly in epidemic and village chickens.
  • Hertz 33 is a velogenic (highly virulent field) strain, not a vaccine strain.
Know More
  • Live lentogenic immunization is also called priming.
  • Inactivated vaccines use formalin or betapropiolactone inactivation.
  • Recombinant vaccines insert F/HN genes into herpesvirus of turkeys.
  • Marker vaccines replace an NP-gene epitope to differentiate infected from vaccinated birds.

posts.post_title: OIE listing status of Newcastle disease
posts.post_content: Along with highly pathogenic avian influenza, Newcastle disease is one of only two poultry diseases specified under which OIE listing?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: List A

Newcastle disease is classified as a List A infection by the OIE.

Correct Option Explanation

ND and highly pathogenic avian influenza are the only two poultry diseases specified as List A, reflecting their severe economic and trade impact.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • List B, List C and List D are not the classification used for ND in the source material; ND is specifically designated List A.
Know More
  • ND risk group is Group II animal pathogen.
  • ND has been reported in at least 241 species of birds.
  • Virus grows in chicken embryo fibroblast and BHK21 cells.
  • Human infection is usually limited to conjunctivitis.

posts.post_title: Which statements about ND diagnosis are correct?
posts.post_content:
Consider the following statements regarding laboratory diagnosis of Newcastle disease:

  1. RT-PCR uses primers targeting the F gene.
  2. The intracerebral pathogenicity index (ICPI) is performed in 6-week-old SPF chickens.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Only 1

Only statement 1 is correct; RT-PCR for NDV uses primers for the F gene.

Correct Option Explanation

Nucleic acid identification of APMV-1 from clinical materials is done by RT-PCR targeting the F gene, as well as nucleic acid probes and antigen-capture ELISA.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Statement 2 is false because the ICPI test uses day-old chicks, not 6-week-old SPF chickens; the 6-week-old SPF chicken test is the IVPI.
Know More
  • ICPI birds are scored over an 8-day period.
  • IVPI birds are scored over a 10-day period.
  • Antigen ELISA types include antigen capture and antigen competitive.
  • VVND-infected chicks typically die in 3 to 7 days on isolation testing.

posts.post_title: Serological test titre indicating recent ND infection
posts.post_content: In the haemagglutination inhibition (HI) test for Newcastle disease antibodies, a titre of log2 6 or more is suggestive of what?

_aimcq_options.text: A recent infection by the virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A recent infection by the virus

An HI titre of log2 6 or more suggests recent NDV infection.

Correct Option Explanation

The HI test relies on HN-mediated agglutination of chicken RBCs being inhibited by specific antibody; a titre of log2 3 is considered indicative of protection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Absence of infection is inconsistent with a high titre, which reflects active antibody response.
  • Vaccine failure and cross-reaction with APMV-2 are not the interpretation given for a titre of log2 6 or more.
Know More
  • Monoclonal antibody-based HI avoids cross-reaction with other APMV serotypes.
  • ELISA detects anti-NDV antibody using an enzyme-conjugated anti-chicken antibody.
  • Virus grows well on pig kidney cells too.
  • Vaccine application methods include mass spray, feed, eye/nasal drops and injection.

posts.post_title: Genus of Rinderpest virus
posts.post_content: Rinderpest virus belongs to which genus, along with measles virus and canine distemper virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morbillivirus

Rinderpest virus belongs to genus Morbillivirus.

Correct Option Explanation

Rinderpest shares structural and antigenic similarity with measles and canine distemper viruses; together they form the MEDIPEST group.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Avulavirus is the genus of Newcastle disease virus, a different paramyxovirus genus.
  • Pneumovirus covers respiratory syncytial-type viruses, unrelated to rinderpest.
  • Lyssavirus is the genus of rabies virus, family Rhabdoviridae.
Know More
  • Rinderpest is differentiated from PPR using N-gene probes.
  • Synonym: Cattle plague.
  • OIE Listing: List A; Risk group Class II.
  • Laboratory animal of choice for growth is the rabbit.

posts.post_title: Protein responsible for cell attachment in rinderpest virus
posts.post_content: Which rinderpest virus protein is responsible for attachment of the virus to the host cell membrane?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Haemagglutinin (H)

The H protein (haemagglutinin) enables the virus to attach to the host cell membrane.

Correct Option Explanation

H is responsible for attachment while the F protein is responsible for entry into the cell via membrane fusion; both are essential for establishing infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Matrix protein (M) links nucleocapsids to envelope glycoproteins to produce virus budding.
  • Fusion protein (F) enables membrane fusion for entry, a distinct role from attachment.
  • Large protein (L) acts as transcriptase/replicase with the P protein, not an attachment protein.
Know More
  • Virus also has two non-structural proteins C/V.
  • Virion measures approximately 100-300 nm.
  • Virus destroyed by 5% sodium hydroxide and 50% lysol in dung.
  • Cultivated in Vero cells and lymphoblastoid line B95a.

posts.post_title: Rinderpest incubation period following natural exposure
posts.post_content: Following natural exposure, the incubation period of rinderpest usually ranges from 3 to 15 days, but is most commonly how many days?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 4 to 5 days

The rinderpest incubation period is usually 4 to 5 days.

Correct Option Explanation

Although the range extends from 3 to 15 days depending on strain, dose and exposure route, 4-5 days is typical following natural exposure.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 1 to 2 days is too short for the documented natural incubation range.
  • 10 to 12 and 20 to 25 days exceed the typical range, though subacute forms may extend up to 15 days.
Know More
  • Acute disease has five phases ending in a convalescent phase.
  • The diarrhoeic phase is called shooting diarrhoea.
  • Death typically occurs 6 to 12 days after prodromal onset.
  • Virus selectively destroys T- and B-lymphocytes in cattle.

posts.post_title: Genus of PPR virus
posts.post_content: Peste des petits ruminants virus (PPRV), closely related to rinderpest virus, belongs to which genus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morbillivirus

PPR virus belongs to genus Morbillivirus, family Paramyxoviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

PPRV is closely related to rinderpest virus but differentiated from it using nucleic acid probes for the N gene.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Avulavirus is the genus for Newcastle disease virus, not PPRV.
  • Pestivirus covers viruses like classical swine fever and BVD virus, family Flaviviridae.
  • Orbivirus covers viruses like bluetongue virus, family Reoviridae.
Know More
  • PPRV virion measures approximately 150 nm.
  • The AR-87 (Arasur) strain is used as a vaccine in Southern India.
  • PPRV is heat sensitive, destroyed at 56°C.
  • PPR causes haemagglutination of chicken RBCs at PBS pH 6.8.

posts.post_title: Primary host species affected by PPR
posts.post_content: PPR is primarily a disease of which host species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sheep and goats

PPR is primarily a disease of sheep and goats.

Correct Option Explanation

Cattle, buffaloes, camels and pigs are also susceptible but do not show clinical signs and cannot transmit the disease to other animals.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cattle and buffaloes are susceptible to infection but remain subclinical, unlike sheep and goats.
  • Horses and donkeys are not documented hosts of PPRV in the source material.
  • Pigs and wild boar are hosts of classical swine fever, not the primary PPR hosts.
Know More
  • PPR is prevalent in Sub-Saharan Africa, Indian subcontinent and Middle East.
  • Incubation period is 4 to 5 days.
  • Mortality in outbreaks ranges 20 to 90%.
  • PPR does not infect humans.

posts.post_title: PPR isolate used as vaccine strain in Southern India
posts.post_content: Which South Indian isolate of PPR virus, developed at the Department of Veterinary Microbiology, Madras Veterinary College, is used as a homologous vaccine strain?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: AR-87 (Arasur)

The AR-87 (Arasur) strain of PPRV is used as a homologous vaccine in Southern India.

Correct Option Explanation

It was developed at the Department of Veterinary Microbiology, Madras Veterinary College and used to control PPR in sheep and goats.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coimbatore (CBE) and Poondi (92) are other South Indian PPRV isolates, but not the vaccine strain named in the source.
  • F strain is a lentogenic vaccine strain of Newcastle disease virus, unrelated to PPR.
Know More
  • Different PPRV strains fall into four antigenic groups.
  • Tissue culture rinderpest vaccine also protects goats against PPR for 12 months.
  • Field diagnosis differentiates PPR from rinderpest, bluetongue, and contagious ecthyma.
  • PPR is treated symptomatically with oxytetracycline for secondary infections.

posts.post_title: Genus of Canine Distemper Virus
posts.post_content: Canine Distemper Virus (CDV) belongs to which genus within the family Paramyxoviridae?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morbillivirus

CDV belongs to genus Morbillivirus within family Paramyxoviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

This genus also includes phocine distemper virus, dolphin morbillivirus, rinderpest virus, PPR virus and measles virus.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Avulavirus covers Newcastle disease virus, not CDV.
  • Lyssavirus covers rabies virus, family Rhabdoviridae.
  • Pneumovirus covers respiratory syncytial-type viruses, unrelated to CDV.
Know More
  • Synonyms: Carre's disease, Hard pad disease.
  • CDV diameter ranges 100-250 nm.
  • Vaccine strain used in India: Rockborn strain.
  • Virus is rapidly inactivated above 32°C.

posts.post_title: Vaccine strain of Canine Distemper Virus used in India
posts.post_content: Which strain of Canine Distemper Virus is used as a vaccine strain in India?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rockborn strain

The Rockborn strain of CDV is used as a vaccine strain in India.

Correct Option Explanation

This live vaccine strain is used to immunize dogs against canine distemper.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • La Sota is a lentogenic vaccine strain of Newcastle disease virus, unrelated to CDV.
  • TC-83 is a live attenuated vaccine strain used for Venezuelan equine encephalitis.
  • Flury is an avianized rabies vaccine strain, not a CDV strain.
Know More
  • CDV grows well in dog kidney, ferret cells and chick fibroblasts.
  • Virus reaches lung lymph nodes within 24 hours of infection.
  • By day 6, virus migrates to spleen, stomach, intestine and liver.
  • Main transmission mode is airborne.

posts.post_title: Mechanism of CDV spread within the host body
posts.post_content: After infecting a dog, canine distemper virus is engulfed by which cell type, which then serves as its means of transportation through the body?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Macrophages

CDV is engulfed by macrophages, which transport it through the host's body.

Correct Option Explanation

The virus is not killed by macrophages; instead it uses them as a transportation vehicle to spread to lymph nodes and other organs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Neutrophils are not described as the transport cell for CDV in the source.
  • Erythrocytes and Platelets are non-phagocytic cells and play no role in CDV dissemination.
Know More
  • Virus persists in CNS and skin after clearance from viscera.
  • CDV causes seizures and skin hardening long-term.
  • Cultivation in eggs shows no CAM changes until the 10th passage.
  • Dogs in recovery may shed virus for several weeks.

posts.post_title: Synonym for canine distemper
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a synonym for canine distemper?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Carre's disease

Carre's disease is a synonym for canine distemper.

Correct Option Explanation

Canine distemper is also known as Carre's disease or Hard pad disease.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Swamp fever is a synonym for equine infectious anaemia, not canine distemper.
  • Cattle plague is a synonym for rinderpest.
  • Mad dog disease (and hydrophobia) refers to rabies, not distemper.
Know More
  • CDV contains six proteins: NP, P, M, F, H, L.
  • CDV is highly stable in cold, dark conditions for months.
  • Infection is more severe in puppies.
  • Hosts include raccoons, skunks and foxes besides dogs.

posts.post_title: CDV survival at sub-zero versus elevated temperature
posts.post_content: Canine distemper virus can remain active for many months at below-zero temperatures, but is rapidly inactivated above what temperature?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 32°C

CDV is rapidly inactivated at temperatures above 32°C.

Correct Option Explanation

At normal temperatures the virus stays active for weeks if protected from sunlight, and for many months below zero, but heat above 32°C destroys it quickly.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 15°C and 22°C are within the range where the virus remains relatively stable, not the inactivation threshold.
  • 45°C exceeds the documented inactivation threshold of 32°C.
Know More
  • Sunlight and routine disinfectants also kill CDV quickly.
  • Distemper viruses can be cultivated in live dogs, ferrets, or suckling mice.
  • CPE in cell culture shows acidophilic intracytoplasmic/intranuclear inclusion bodies.
  • CDV shares antigenic similarity with rinderpest and PPR viruses.

posts.post_title: CDV structural proteins
posts.post_content: How many structural proteins does canine distemper virus (CDV) contain?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Six

CDV contains six structural proteins.

Correct Option Explanation

These are nucleocapsid protein (NP), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), fusion protein (F), haemagglutinin (H) and the large-polymerase protein (L).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Four, five and eight are not the documented protein count for CDV; the virus specifically has six named structural proteins.
Know More
  • CDV is spherical, 100-250 nm in diameter.
  • Genome is negative-sense, non-segmented RNA.
  • Transmission is mainly via respiratory secretions.
  • Fever develops as virus reaches viscera by day 6.

posts.post_title: Number of gene segments in influenza A viruses
posts.post_content: How many separate gene segments does the influenza A virus genome contain, allowing reassortment between viruses from different species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Eight

Influenza A viruses have eight separate gene segments.

Correct Option Explanation

This segmented genome allows viruses from different species (e.g. pig and bird) infecting the same host to reassort, producing new virus combinations.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Four and six segments are incorrect counts; influenza A specifically has eight.
  • Ten segments corresponds to bluetongue virus (Reoviridae), not influenza A.
Know More
  • Major change in surface proteins is called antigenic shift.
  • Pigs can act as a 'mixing vessel' intermediate host.
  • Human infection strains include H5N1, H7N7, H9N2.
  • HPAI morbidity/mortality can reach 100% within 2-12 days.

posts.post_title: Kidney appearance in laying hens affected by HPAI
posts.post_content: In layers affected by highly pathogenic avian influenza, the peritoneal cavity is often filled with what substance from ruptured ova, causing severe airsacculitis and peritonitis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Yolk

The peritoneal cavity fills with yolk from ruptured ova in affected layers.

Correct Option Explanation

The ovary may be haemorrhagic or degenerated, and yolk from ruptured ova causes severe airsacculitis and peritonitis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bile is not the substance described filling the peritoneal cavity in HPAI-affected layers.
  • Fibrin only understates the finding; yolk material specifically is described, not just fibrin.
  • Urates are deposited in kidney tubules due to congestion, a separate lesion from the peritoneal finding.
Know More
  • Incubation period is 3 to 7 days.
  • Field diagnosis suggested by facial edema and cyanotic combs.
  • Isolation uses 9-11 day old embryonated eggs.
  • Amantadine hydrochloride gives symptomatic relief but induces resistance.

posts.post_title: Route of avian influenza virus isolation in eggs
posts.post_content: Which route of inoculation into embryonated eggs is used to isolate avian influenza virus, followed by confirmation via HA activity and AGID?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Chorioallantoic membrane route

Samples are centrifuged and the supernatant inoculated into eggs, with virus confirmed through the allantoic fluid.

Correct Option Explanation

Presence of virus in allantoic fluid is confirmed by HA activity, AGID, RT-PCR, and antigen-capture ELISA after incubation at 35-37°C for 4 days.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Amniotic route is used for isolation of some other viruses like equine influenza, not the described AI protocol.
  • Chorioallantoic membrane route as a distinct term is used for pox and herpesviruses in this material, not for AI virus isolation via allantoic fluid.
  • Intravenous route into the embryo is not the described AI virus isolation method.
Know More
  • Samples come from cloacal swabs, trachea, lungs, air sacs.
  • PBS used is isotonic at pH 7.0-7.4.
  • Differential diagnosis includes VVND and infectious laryngotracheitis.
  • Vaccination may use recombinant fowl pox carrying the H5 gene.

posts.post_title: Genus of equine influenza virus
posts.post_content: Equine influenza virus belongs to which genus of the family Orthomyxoviridae?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type A Influenza virus

Equine influenza virus belongs to genus Type A Influenza virus.

Correct Option Explanation

It is caused by two subtypes, H7N7 (formerly equi-1) and H3N8 (formerly equi-2), both under the genus Influenzavirus A.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Type B and Type C Influenza viruses are not the genus responsible for equine influenza in the source material.
  • Thogotovirus is a different Orthomyxoviridae genus, unrelated to equine influenza.
Know More
  • Cultivation uses MDCK cell line and embryonated eggs.
  • OIE listing: List B disease.
  • Incubation period is very short, 1-5 days.
  • Cough may persist around 10 days.

posts.post_title: Aerosol transmission distance of equine influenza
posts.post_content: Equine influenza can spread by aerosol from coughing over what approximate distance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Up to 30 m

Aerosol from coughing can spread equine influenza up to 30 m.

Correct Option Explanation

Additionally, wind can carry the virus up to 8 km, and indirect contact with infected material also spreads infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Up to 5 m understates the documented aerosol spread distance.
  • Up to 100 m and up to 1 km overstate the aerosol distance; 1 km approaches the wind-spread figure of 8 km, but is not the specific aerosol figure.
Know More
  • Infected animals shed virus for about 8 days.
  • Fever reaches approximately 38.9°C.
  • Killed vaccine doses given 3-6 weeks apart from 6 months of age.
  • Attenuated live intranasal vaccine (AE-2) protects for 6 months.

posts.post_title: Number of haemagglutinin and neuraminidase types in swine influenza
posts.post_content: How many haemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) types are recognised for classifying influenza viruses such as those causing swine influenza?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 13 H and 9 N types

There are 13 H and 9 N types recognised for influenza classification.

Correct Option Explanation

Variations in HA and NA classify the virus into many subtypes; common swine influenza strains belong to H1N1, H3N2 and H1N2.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 9 H and 13 N types reverses the correct figures.
  • 8 H and 8 N types and 16 H and 16 N types are not the figures given in the source material for this course.
Know More
  • The 4th RNA segment codes for HA, the 6th for NA.
  • SIV agglutinates chicken and turkey RBCs.
  • Incubation period as short as 4 hours in severe epidemics.
  • Mortality is usually about 1%.

posts.post_title: Cell culture systems preferred for swine influenza virus growth
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a preferred cell culture system for growth of swine influenza virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Madin-Darby Canine Kidney (MDCK) cells

MDCK cells are a preferred system for swine influenza virus growth.

Correct Option Explanation

Other preferred systems include swine kidney, swine testicle or swine lung epithelial cell lines, with CPE appearing after 7 days.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vero cells are used for viruses like rinderpest and PPR, not the preferred SIV system here.
  • BHK-21 cells are used for FMD and rabies virus cultivation, not SIV.
  • PK-15 cells are used for classical swine fever and pseudorabies virus, not SIV.
Know More
  • Virus also grows in 9-11 day old embryonated eggs.
  • HA test uses 0.5% chicken or turkey RBCs.
  • Virus can be shed for 30 days post-infection.
  • Outbreaks are typically seasonal, late autumn and early winter.

posts.post_title: Genus of rabies virus
posts.post_content: Rabies virus, transmissible to all mammals, belongs to which genus of family Rhabdoviridae?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lyssavirus

Rabies virus is a neurotropic virus of genus Lyssavirus, family Rhabdoviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

There are seven distinct genetic lineages of lyssaviruses, including classical rabies virus (RABV), Lagos bat virus and Mokola virus.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ephemerovirus is the genus of bovine ephemeral fever virus, not rabies.
  • Vesiculovirus covers other rhabdoviruses like vesicular stomatitis virus, not rabies.
  • Morbillivirus covers rinderpest, PPR and CDV, a paramyxovirus genus unrelated to rabies.
Know More
  • Rabies virus is bullet-shaped, approximately 180 nm long.
  • Genome encodes five proteins: N, P, M, G, L.
  • Synonyms include hydrophobia, mad dog disease.
  • OIE Listing: List A; Risk group III.

posts.post_title: Characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusion in rabies-infected neurons
posts.post_content: What are the round or oval cytoplasmic inclusions found within nerve cells of rabies-infected animals, especially in the pyramidal cells of Ammon's horn?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Negri bodies

Negri bodies are the characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions of rabies infection.

Correct Option Explanation

They vary in size from 0.25 to 27 µm, are found most frequently in pyramidal cells of Ammon's horn and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum, and appear magenta with Sellers or Mann's stain.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bollinger bodies are inclusion bodies seen in fowlpox virus infection, unrelated to rabies.
  • Guarnieri bodies are associated with vaccinia/variola infections, not covered as a rabies finding here.
  • Babes nodules are glial cell aggregates also seen in rabies, but distinct from the cytoplasmic Negri bodies themselves.
Know More
  • Rabies is most abundant in thalamus, pons and medulla.
  • FAT is the most widely used diagnostic test, per WHO and OIE.
  • Mouse inoculation test shows paralysis/death within 28 days.
  • Neuroblastoma line CCL-131 is used for isolation.

posts.post_title: Most widely used rabies diagnostic test recommended by WHO and OIE
posts.post_content: Which test is the most widely used method for rabies diagnosis and is recommended by both WHO and OIE?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Fluorescent antibody test

The fluorescent antibody test (FAT) is the most widely used method, recommended by WHO and OIE.

Correct Option Explanation

Since rabies virus does not haemagglutinate, direct antigen detection methods like FAT on brain, salivary gland or saliva samples are preferred.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • AGID is used for infections such as EIA (Coggins test) and Marek's disease, not as the primary rabies test.
  • Complement fixation test is used for FMD and equine encephalitis serology, not the primary rabies diagnostic tool.
  • HI test cannot be used for rabies because the virus does not haemagglutinate.
Know More
  • ELISA for rabies is called RREID.
  • FAVN test is accepted for international trade.
  • RFFIT determines rabies-neutralising antibody.
  • Fixed viruses lose ability to form Negri bodies.

posts.post_title: Typical incubation period of rabies in dogs
posts.post_content: Most cases of rabies in dogs occur within what time frame after exposure?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 21 to 80 days

Most cases in dogs occur within 21 to 80 days after exposure.

Correct Option Explanation

The incubation period is both prolonged and variable, and may be shorter or considerably longer than this typical range depending on factors like bite location and viral dose.

Incorrect Options Analysis

  • Synonym: Hog cholera.

posts.post_title: Virus antigenically related to classical swine fever virus
posts.post_content: Classical swine fever virus is antigenically closely related to which other pestivirus, often complicating serological diagnosis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bovine viral diarrhoea virus

CSF virus is antigenically closely related to bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV).

Correct Option Explanation

Both belong to genus Pestivirus, and this cross-reactivity can cause false-positive results in serological tests for CSF unless carefully controlled.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • African swine fever virus, despite clinically similar disease, is taxonomically unrelated (family Asfarviridae) and does not cross-react serologically with CSFV.
  • Rinderpest virus is a morbillivirus, unrelated to pestiviruses.
  • FMD virus is a picornavirus, structurally and antigenically distinct from CSFV.
Know More
  • Differential diagnosis between CSF and ASF requires laboratory confirmation.
  • Clinical signs of CSF include fever, purple skin discoloration, and high mortality in piglets.
  • Vaccination uses live attenuated strains like the Chinese (C) strain.
  • Cultivation is done in PK-15 cell line.

posts.post_title: Cell line used for cultivation of classical swine fever virus
posts.post_content: Which cell line is used for cultivation and isolation of classical swine fever virus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: PK-15 cells

PK-15 (pig kidney) cells are used for CSF virus cultivation.

Correct Option Explanation

Unlike many other viruses, CSFV usually produces no visible cytopathic effect, so infection is confirmed by immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • BHK-21 cells are typically used for FMD and rabies virus, not the preferred CSFV cell line here.
  • MDCK cells are used for influenza virus cultivation, not CSFV.
  • CEF (chicken embryo fibroblast) cells are used for Newcastle disease and Marek's disease viruses, not CSFV.
Know More
  • CSFV is non-cytopathic in cell culture, requiring special detection methods.
  • Fluorescent antibody test on tonsil sections is a rapid diagnostic tool.
  • Chronic infection can lead to persistently infected, immunotolerant piglets.
  • The C-strain vaccine provides good protective immunity.

posts.post_title: Cytopathic effect of classical swine fever virus in cell culture
posts.post_content: Unlike many other RNA viruses, classical swine fever virus typically shows what characteristic in routine cell culture?

_aimcq_options.text: Formation of large intranuclear inclusion bodies

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: No visible cytopathic effect

CSF virus is typically non-cytopathic in cell culture.

Correct Option Explanation

Because no visible CPE occurs, infection is confirmed indirectly using immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining rather than by observing cell damage under a microscope.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rapid syncytia formation is characteristic of other viruses like some paramyxoviruses, not CSFV.
  • Large intranuclear inclusion bodies are typical of herpesviruses, not CSFV.
  • Complete cell lysis within 24 hours does not match CSFV's typically silent growth pattern.
Know More

  • Congenital tremor can occur in piglets born to infected sows.
  • Chronic CSF can mimic other diseases, complicating clinical diagnosis.

posts.post_title: Synonym for classical swine fever
posts.post_content: Classical swine fever is also commonly known by which other name?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Hog cholera

Classical swine fever is also known as hog cholera.

Correct Option Explanation

This synonym is widely used, especially in older literature and in regions like the United States.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Swine erysipelas is a bacterial disease caused by Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, unrelated to CSF.
  • Blue ear disease is a synonym for porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome (PRRS), not CSF.
  • Aujeszky's disease is caused by a herpesvirus (pseudorabies virus), a distinct disease from CSF.
Know More

posts.post_title: Characteristic intestinal lesion in chronic classical swine fever
posts.post_content: In chronic cases of classical swine fever, characteristic circular, layered ulcers may be found in the large intestine, referred to as what?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Button ulcers

Chronic CSF cases show characteristic button ulcers in the large intestine.

Correct Option Explanation

These are circular, layered ulcers, often centred over Peyer's patches or lymphoid follicles, formed by concentric rings of necrotic tissue.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Rose spots' is a term associated with typhoid fever skin lesions in humans, not swine fever intestinal lesions.
  • 'Ammon's horn lesions' relate to rabies virus neuropathology, not CSF.
  • 'Bollinger bodies' are inclusion bodies of fowlpox virus infection, unrelated to CSF.
Know More
  • Chronic CSF can last for weeks to months before death.
  • Skin haemorrhages give a purplish discoloration, especially on ears, snout, and abdomen.
  • Lymphoid depletion and thymic atrophy are common histological findings.
  • OIE-recognised control includes stamping-out policies in non-endemic countries.

posts.post_title: Consequence of transplacental infection with CSF virus
posts.post_content: When a pregnant sow is infected with certain strains of classical swine fever virus, what can result in the piglets born to her?

_aimcq_options.text: Resistance to all future picornavirus infections

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Persistently infected, immunotolerant carrier piglets

Transplacental infection can produce persistently infected, immunotolerant piglets.

Correct Option Explanation

These piglets may appear clinically normal at birth but continuously shed virus, playing a major role in maintaining and spreading infection within a herd, similar to the mechanism seen with BVDV.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complete natural immunity is the opposite of what occurs — these piglets are immunotolerant, not protected.
  • Resistance to picornavirus infections is unrelated, since CSFV is a pestivirus (Flaviviridae), not a picornavirus.
  • 'Sterile, non-infectious piglets' contradicts the persistent-shedding nature of these carrier animals.
Know More
  • Persistently infected animals are a key obstacle to CSF eradication programs.
  • Congenital tremor ('shaking pig disease') can also occur in affected litters.
  • Similar immunotolerant carrier states occur with BVDV in cattle.
  • Identification of carriers requires antigen or nucleic acid-based testing, since antibody may be absent.

posts.post_title: Genus and family of bovine viral diarrhoea virus
posts.post_content: Bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV) belongs to which genus and family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Genus Pestivirus, family Flaviviridae

BVDV belongs to genus Pestivirus, family Flaviviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

It is antigenically closely related to classical swine fever virus and border disease virus, both in the same genus.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Morbillivirus/Paramyxoviridae covers rinderpest, PPR and CDV, not BVDV.
  • Orbivirus/Reoviridae covers bluetongue and African horse sickness viruses.
  • Coronavirus/Coronaviridae covers infectious bronchitis and TGE viruses, structurally distinct from BVDV.
Know More
  • Two biotypes exist: cytopathic and non-cytopathic.
  • BVDV causes mucosal disease when both biotypes co-infect a persistently infected animal.
  • Persistently infected (PI) calves result from fetal infection with the non-cytopathic biotype before immunocompetence develops.
  • OIE and national control programs target elimination of PI animals.

posts.post_title: Biotypes of bovine viral diarrhoea virus
posts.post_content: How many biotypes of bovine viral diarrhoea virus are recognised, based on their effect in cell culture?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Two

BVDV exists as two biotypes: cytopathic and non-cytopathic.

Correct Option Explanation

The non-cytopathic biotype is responsible for establishing persistent infection in the fetus, while co-infection with the cytopathic biotype in a PI animal triggers fatal mucosal disease.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • One biotype does not account for the distinct cytopathic/non-cytopathic classification described.
  • Three and four biotypes overstate the documented classification, which is specifically two.
Know More
  • BVDV has two genotypes as well, BVDV-1 and BVDV-2.
  • Clinical BVD in immunocompetent cattle is usually mild.
  • Fetal infection timing determines the outcome: abortion, malformation, or PI calf.
  • Mucosal disease is characterised by severe erosive lesions of the GI tract and is invariably fatal.

posts.post_title: Mechanism producing persistently infected (PI) calves in BVD
posts.post_content: Persistently infected (PI) calves in bovine viral diarrhoea arise when the fetus is infected with which biotype of BVDV before it becomes immunocompetent?

_aimcq_options.text: Neither biotype; PI arises after birth

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Non-cytopathic biotype

Fetal infection with the non-cytopathic biotype before immunocompetence develops leads to persistent infection.

Correct Option Explanation

The fetus recognises the virus as 'self' and becomes immunotolerant, so the calf is born persistently infected, continuously shedding virus for life.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The cytopathic biotype is not the one associated with establishing persistent infection; it is instead linked to triggering mucosal disease in an already-PI animal.
  • Co-infection with both biotypes causes fatal mucosal disease, not the PI state itself.
  • PI specifically arises from in utero infection, not after birth.
Know More
  • PI animals are the main reservoir maintaining BVDV in cattle populations.
  • PI cattle often appear clinically normal but are smaller and less thrifty.
  • Testing programs use ear-notch antigen ELISA or PCR to identify PI calves.
  • Removal of PI animals is central to BVD eradication schemes.

posts.post_title: Cause of fatal mucosal disease in BVD
posts.post_content: Fatal mucosal disease in a persistently infected (PI) calf typically develops after what event?

_aimcq_options.text: Superinfection with the cytopathic biotype of BVDV
Vaccination with a killed rabies vaccine
Weaning from milk to solid feed

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Superinfection with the cytopathic biotype of BVDV

Mucosal disease develops after superinfection of a PI animal with the cytopathic biotype of BVDV.

Correct Option Explanation

This may occur through exogenous infection or mutation of the animal's own persistent non-cytopathic virus; the resulting disease is invariably fatal, with severe erosive lesions throughout the GI tract.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rabies vaccination is unrelated to BVDV pathogenesis and does not trigger mucosal disease.
  • Cold stress alone is not the documented trigger; specific cytopathic biotype superinfection is required.
  • Weaning is a normal management event, not a described trigger for mucosal disease.
Know More
  • Mucosal disease is characterised by profuse diarrhoea, oral erosions, and high mortality.
  • PI animals with mucosal disease die within days to weeks of onset.
  • Mucosal disease is a hallmark, unique feature of BVDV pathogenesis compared to other pestiviruses.
  • Control focuses on preventing new PI animals via vaccination and biosecurity.

posts.post_title: Reproductive consequences of BVDV infection in pregnant cattle
posts.post_content: Depending on the stage of gestation at which infection occurs, BVDV infection in pregnant cattle can result in which of the following outcomes?

_aimcq_options.text: Only normal, unaffected calves regardless of timing
Embryonic death, abortion, congenital defects, or a persistently infected calf
Immediate maternal death in all cases
Sterility of the dam for life

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Embryonic death, abortion, congenital defects, or a persistently infected calf

Outcomes vary widely: embryonic death, abortion, congenital defects, or a PI calf, depending on gestational timing.

Correct Option Explanation

Early gestational infection often causes embryonic death or abortion, mid-gestation infection can cause congenital defects (e.g. cerebellar hypoplasia) or a PI calf, and late-gestation infection often results in a normal, immunocompetent calf.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Only normal, unaffected calves' ignores the well-documented range of adverse outcomes with early/mid-gestation infection.
  • Immediate maternal death is not a typical feature of BVDV infection in cows.
  • Permanent maternal sterility is not a documented consequence of BVDV infection.
Know More
  • Cerebellar hypoplasia is a classic congenital defect linked to BVDV.
  • Eye defects and skeletal deformities can also occur with fetal infection.
  • Vaccination programs aim to protect the dam before or during early pregnancy.
  • BVDV control emphasises testing and removal of PI animals from the herd.

posts.post_title: Genotypes recognised within BVDV
posts.post_content: Besides the cytopathic and non-cytopathic biotypes, BVDV is also classified into which two genotypes?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: BVDV-1 and BVDV-2

BVDV is further classified into genotypes BVDV-1 and BVDV-2.

Correct Option Explanation

Both genotypes can occur as either cytopathic or non-cytopathic biotypes, and both can cause a spectrum of disease from mild to severe.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Type O and Type A' describes FMD serotypes, not BVDV genotypes.
  • 'Serotype 1 and Serotype 25' resembles the bluetongue virus serotype scheme, not BVDV.
  • 'H1N1 and H3N2' are influenza subtype designations, unrelated to BVDV.
Know More
  • BVDV-2 strains can be associated with more severe acute disease outbreaks.
  • Vaccines ideally provide cross-protection against both genotypes.
  • Genotyping uses molecular sequencing of conserved genome regions.
  • BVDV causes major economic losses through reproductive failure and reduced productivity.

posts.post_title: Primary method for identifying persistently infected cattle
posts.post_content: Which of the following is the primary diagnostic approach for identifying persistently infected (PI) cattle within a herd for BVD control?

_aimcq_options.text: Ear-notch antigen ELISA or PCR testing

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ear-notch antigen ELISA or PCR testing

Ear-notch antigen ELISA or PCR testing is used to identify PI animals.

Correct Option Explanation

Since PI calves may appear clinically normal, laboratory testing of skin/ear-notch samples for viral antigen or nucleic acid is essential to reliably detect and remove carriers.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Physical examination alone is unreliable since PI animals often show no distinguishing clinical signs.
  • Milk fat percentage is unrelated to BVDV infection status.
  • Skin fold thickness testing is used for tuberculosis screening, not BVD.
Know More
  • Bulk milk PCR testing can screen dairy herds for BVDV circulation.
  • Newborn calves are commonly tested before entering the herd.
  • Test-and-cull strategies, combined with vaccination, are used in eradication programs.

posts.post_title: Family classification of infectious bronchitis virus
posts.post_content: Avian infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) belongs to which virus family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Coronaviridae

IBV belongs to family Coronaviridae, genus Gammacoronavirus.

Correct Option Explanation

It is an enveloped, positive-sense RNA virus with characteristic club-shaped spike (S) projections giving a crown-like appearance under electron microscopy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Paramyxoviridae covers Newcastle disease virus, a different respiratory pathogen of poultry.
  • Orthomyxoviridae covers avian influenza virus, unrelated to IBV taxonomically.
  • Reoviridae covers viruses like infectious bursal disease-related viruses, unrelated to IBV.
Know More
  • IBV primarily targets the respiratory tract, but also affects kidneys and the reproductive tract.
  • Nephropathogenic strains cause severe kidney damage in young chicks.
  • Many serotypes exist, with limited cross-protection between them.
  • Vaccination is a major control strategy, using live attenuated and inactivated vaccines.

posts.post_title: Organs targeted by nephropathogenic strains of IBV
posts.post_content: Besides the respiratory tract, nephropathogenic strains of infectious bronchitis virus primarily damage which organ?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Kidneys

Nephropathogenic IBV strains cause severe damage to the kidneys.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected birds show swollen, pale kidneys with urate deposits in the tubules, leading to visceral gout in severe cases, in addition to respiratory signs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The liver is not the primary target of nephropathogenic IBV strains.
  • The spleen is not the described target organ for these strains.
  • The pancreas is not documented as a target organ for IBV in this material.
Know More
  • IBV also affects the oviduct, causing permanent damage in young pullets and false layers.
  • Egg production and quality drop significantly during outbreaks.
  • Diagnosis uses virus isolation in embryonated eggs, RT-PCR, and serology.
  • Multiple serotypes complicate effective vaccination strategies.

posts.post_title: Reproductive tract consequence of IBV infection in young pullets
posts.post_content: Infection of very young pullets with infectious bronchitis virus can cause permanent damage to the oviduct, resulting in birds that mature into what condition?

_aimcq_options.text: Sterile males unable to fertilise eggs
Birds with enhanced future egg production
Birds immune to all future viral infections

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 'False layers' that never lay normally

Affected pullets can mature into 'false layers' that never lay normally due to permanent oviduct damage.

Correct Option Explanation

This occurs when the virus damages the developing oviduct in very young chicks, before the reproductive tract is fully formed, leading to cystic or non-functional oviducts.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Male sterility is not the documented consequence, as the oviduct damage specifically affects female reproductive function.
  • Enhanced future egg production is the opposite of the actual, damaging outcome.
  • Immunity to all future viral infections is not a described consequence of this specific tissue damage.
Know More
  • IBV spreads rapidly by the respiratory route within a flock.

  • Secondary bacterial infections can worsen respiratory outcomes.
  • Vaccination programs use both live and inactivated vaccine combinations.

posts.post_title: Structural feature giving coronaviruses their name
posts.post_content: The name 'coronavirus' derives from the appearance of the virus particle under electron microscopy, which resembles what?

_aimcq_options.text: A solar corona (crown), due to club-shaped spike projections
A brick-shaped particle with lateral bodies
A helical filament with no envelope

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A solar corona (crown), due to club-shaped spike projections

Coronaviruses are named for their resemblance to a solar corona due to club-shaped spike projections.

Correct Option Explanation

These spike (S) glycoprotein projections radiate from the envelope surface, giving a crown-like appearance under electron microscopy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A bullet shape describes rhabdoviruses like rabies virus, not coronaviruses.
  • A brick-shaped particle with lateral bodies describes poxviruses, structurally very different.
  • Coronaviruses are enveloped, so 'no envelope' is incorrect.

  • IBV genome is a large positive-sense single-stranded RNA.
  • Other important coronaviruses include TGE virus of pigs.
  • Cross-protection between IBV serotypes is often poor.
  • Biosecurity and multivalent vaccination programs help manage IBV in flocks.

posts.post_title: Clinical signs of infectious bronchitis in young chicks
posts.post_content: Which set of clinical signs is most characteristic of infectious bronchitis in young chicks?

_aimcq_options.text: Sudden death with no respiratory signs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Gasping, coughing, and nasal discharge

Young chicks with infectious bronchitis typically show gasping, coughing, and nasal discharge.

Correct Option Explanation

The disease spreads rapidly by the respiratory route through a flock, and severe cases can also involve tracheal rales audible on close observation.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sudden death with no respiratory signs does not match the typical, primarily respiratory presentation.

  • Egg production and shell quality both drop in laying flocks during outbreaks.

posts.post_title: Impact of IBV on egg production and shell quality
posts.post_content: Infection of laying hens with infectious bronchitis virus commonly causes which effect on egg production?

_aimcq_options.text: A sharp drop in egg production and poor shell quality
A permanent increase in egg production
No effect on egg production or shell quality
Only an increase in egg size with no other change

Correct Answer: A sharp drop in egg production and poor shell quality

  • A permanent increase in egg production is the opposite of the documented harmful effect.

  • An increase in egg size alone does not capture the actual quality decline seen with IBV.

  • Recovery of egg production may be incomplete even after clinical recovery.

posts.post_title: Family classification of TGE virus
posts.post_content: Transmissible gastroenteritis (TGE) virus of pigs belongs to which family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Coronaviridae

TGE virus belongs to family Coronaviridae, genus Alphacoronavirus.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes severe, often fatal diarrhoea in very young piglets, and shares antigenic similarity with porcine respiratory coronavirus (PRCV).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Picornaviridae covers FMD virus, structurally and taxonomically distinct from TGE virus.

  • Parvoviridae covers canine and porcine parvoviruses, small DNA viruses unrelated to TGE virus.

  • Mortality can approach 100% in piglets under 2 weeks of age.
  • Older pigs generally show milder disease and recover.

  • Vaccination and colostral immunity are key control measures.

posts.post_title: Age group most severely affected by transmissible gastroenteritis
posts.post_content: Transmissible gastroenteritis causes the highest mortality, approaching 100%, in which age group of pigs?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Piglets under 2 weeks of age

Mortality approaches 100% in piglets under 2 weeks of age.

Correct Option Explanation

Older pigs typically show milder, self-limiting diarrhoea and recover, reflecting age-related susceptibility to this coronavirus.

  • Finisher pigs and adult boars generally experience much milder disease compared to very young piglets.

  • Vomiting and profuse watery diarrhoea are classic clinical signs.

posts.post_title: Naturally occurring deletion mutant related to TGE virus
posts.post_content: Porcine respiratory coronavirus (PRCV) arose naturally as a deletion mutant of which virus, but with altered tissue tropism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: TGE virus

PRCV arose as a naturally occurring deletion mutant of TGE virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite being closely related, PRCV has tropism mainly for the respiratory tract rather than the intestine, causing milder disease than classical TGE.

  • Classical swine fever virus is a pestivirus, taxonomically unrelated to TGE virus.

posts.post_title: Primary cause of death in piglets with transmissible gastroenteritis
posts.post_content: What is the primary cause of death in young piglets severely affected by transmissible gastroenteritis?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Severe dehydration from profuse diarrhoea

Severe dehydration resulting from profuse watery diarrhoea is the primary cause of death.

Correct Option Explanation

Vomiting compounds fluid loss, and very young piglets have limited physiological reserve, so rapid, severe dehydration quickly becomes fatal.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Acute liver failure is not the described mechanism of death in TGE.
  • Cardiac arrhythmia is not documented as the primary cause of death in this disease.
  • Respiratory failure from pneumonia is more characteristic of PRCV, not classical enteric TGE.
Know More
  • Supportive fluid therapy can help reduce mortality in mild-to-moderate cases.
  • Colostral antibody, transferred via milk (lactogenic immunity), is a key protective factor.
  • Herds with endemic exposure often show reduced clinical severity over time.
  • Diagnosis uses virus isolation, RT-PCR, or immunofluorescence on intestinal tissue.

posts.post_title: Route of protective immunity against TGE in suckling piglets
posts.post_content: The main source of early protective immunity against transmissible gastroenteritis in suckling piglets is which of the following?

_aimcq_options.text: Lactogenic (colostrum and milk-derived) antibody from the sow
Active immunity developed entirely by the piglet's own immune system at birth
Antibody transferred across the placenta only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Lactogenic (colostrum and milk-derived) antibody from the sow

Lactogenic immunity, via colostrum and milk antibody from the sow, is the key protective factor.

Since piglets are born with an immature immune system, maternal antibody in colostrum and ongoing milk secretion provides critical passive protection against intestinal infection during the vulnerable early weeks.

  • The piglet's own active immunity is not yet developed enough at birth to provide adequate protection.

  • Antibiotics have no effect against this viral disease.
Know More
  • Sow vaccination programs aim to boost colostral antibody levels before farrowing.
  • Piglets weaned too early lose this protection and become more vulnerable.
  • Biosecurity measures reduce introduction of the virus onto naive farms.
  • Recovered sows can develop long-lasting immunity that benefits future litters.

posts.post_title: Species specificity of transmissible gastroenteritis virus
posts.post_content: Transmissible gastroenteritis virus is primarily a pathogen of which animal species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pigs

TGE virus is primarily a pathogen of pigs, especially young piglets.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes severe enteric disease with vomiting and diarrhoea, most devastating in piglets under two weeks of age.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cattle are affected by a different coronavirus (bovine coronavirus), not TGE virus.
  • Poultry are affected by infectious bronchitis virus, a different coronavirus genus.
  • Horses are not a documented host for TGE virus in this material.
Know More
  • TGE is a major economic concern in intensive pig-rearing operations.

  • All-in/all-out management practices help reduce transmission risk.
  • Both TGEV and PRCV are considered when interpreting serological surveys.

posts.post_title: Genus and family of bluetongue virus
posts.post_content: Bluetongue virus belongs to which genus and family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Genus Orbivirus, family Reoviridae

Bluetongue virus belongs to genus Orbivirus, family Reoviridae.

It has a non-enveloped, icosahedral capsid with a segmented double-stranded RNA genome, and is transmitted by Culicoides midges.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pestivirus/Flaviviridae covers CSF and BVD viruses, unrelated to bluetongue virus.

posts.post_title: Primary vector for bluetongue virus transmission
posts.post_content: Bluetongue virus is primarily transmitted between ruminants by which biting insect?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Culicoides midges

Bluetongue virus is transmitted primarily by Culicoides biting midges.

Correct Option Explanation

The virus replicates within the midge before transmission, making these insects true biological vectors, and disease incidence closely tracks midge activity and distribution.

  • Ixodes ticks are not the documented vector for bluetongue virus.

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
