Fowlpox presents as either the cutaneous (dry) form or the more serious diphtheritic (wet) form.

Correct Option Explanation

The dry form causes wart-like nodules on unfeathered skin like the comb and wattles, while the wet form produces lesions in the mouth, oesophagus, and trachea that can obstruct breathing and feeding.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 'Peracute and chronic latent form' is not the standard clinical classification described for fowlpox.
  • 'Congenital and acquired form' is not the documented classification for this disease.
  • 'Nervous and enteric form' does not match the described cutaneous/diphtheritic classification of fowlpox.
Know More
  • The diphtheritic form can cause significant mortality due to respiratory obstruction.
  • Bollinger bodies are the characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions seen histologically.
  • Live vaccines, often via wing-web stab, are used for control.
  • Good mosquito control reduces mechanical transmission on farms.

posts.post_title: Genus of orf (contagious ecthyma) virus
posts.post_content: Orf virus, causing contagious ecthyma in sheep and goats, belongs to which genus?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parapoxvirus

Orf virus belongs to genus Parapoxvirus, family Poxviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes proliferative, scabby lesions typically around the lips and mouth of young sheep and goats, and is notably zoonotic.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Capripoxvirus covers sheep pox and goat pox viruses, distinct and generally more severe diseases than orf.
  • Avipoxvirus covers fowlpox virus, a bird-specific genus.
  • Orthopoxvirus covers cowpox and vaccinia viruses, a different genus.
Know More
  • Synonym: Contagious pustular dermatitis / soremouth.
  • Lesions typically resolve within 3-4 weeks without treatment.
  • Zoonotic transmission to humans (shepherds, vets) causes localised skin lesions on hands.
  • Live vaccines are used in endemic flocks, applied to scarified skin.

posts.post_title: Typical location of orf lesions in young sheep and goats
posts.post_content: Contagious ecthyma (orf) typically produces proliferative scabby lesions in which location on young sheep and goats?

_aimcq_options.text: On the tongue and hard palate exclusively
On the internal organs only, with no skin involvement

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Around the lips and mouth

Orf lesions typically occur around the lips and mouth of young sheep and goats.

Correct Option Explanation

The proliferative, wart-like scabs can interfere with suckling and grazing, sometimes leading to secondary complications such as reduced growth or mastitis in nursing dams from lamb-to-udder transfer.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Lesions are not restricted exclusively to the tongue and hard palate; the lips and mouth area is the classic site.
  • The ears are not the primary or classic site of orf lesions.
  • Orf is fundamentally a skin (cutaneous) disease, so 'no skin involvement' is incorrect.
Know More
  • Lesions can occasionally spread to the udder of nursing ewes, causing painful mastitis.
  • The disease is usually self-limiting, resolving within a few weeks.
  • Good hygiene practices reduce zoonotic transmission risk to handlers.
  • Recovered animals typically develop solid, long-lasting immunity.

posts.post_title: Genus of cowpox and buffalopox viruses
posts.post_content: Cowpox virus and buffalopox virus belong to which genus of family Poxviridae?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Orthopoxvirus

Cowpox and buffalopox viruses belong to genus Orthopoxvirus, the same genus as vaccinia and variola (smallpox) viruses.

Correct Option Explanation

Both are zoonotic, causing localised pustular lesions primarily on the teats and udder of milking animals, which can then transfer to milkers' hands.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Capripoxvirus covers sheep pox, goat pox and lumpy skin disease viruses, a different genus.
  • Parapoxvirus covers orf and pseudocowpox viruses, a distinct genus from Orthopoxvirus.
  • Avipoxvirus covers fowlpox virus, specific to birds.
Know More
  • Cowpox is now rare in cattle but persists in some rodent reservoirs in Europe.
  • Buffalopox has caused notable outbreaks among milk handlers in South Asia.
  • Both diseases are generally self-limiting in humans, causing localised skin lesions.
  • Good milking hygiene reduces zoonotic transmission risk.

posts.post_title: Zoonotic potential of orf, cowpox and buffalopox viruses
posts.post_content: Orf virus, cowpox virus and buffalopox virus share what important public health characteristic?

_aimcq_options.text: All three are zoonotic, capable of causing skin lesions in humans
None of the three can infect humans under any circumstances
All three cause fatal systemic disease in every infected human
All three require mosquito bites to infect humans

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: All three are zoonotic, capable of causing skin lesions in humans

Orf, cowpox, and buffalopox viruses are all zoonotic, typically causing localised skin lesions in exposed people.

Correct Option Explanation

Farmers, shepherds, veterinarians, and milkers who handle infected animals or contaminated material are at greatest risk of acquiring these usually self-limiting infections through direct skin contact.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • All three viruses are documented to infect humans through direct contact, contradicting 'none can infect humans'.
  • Human infections with these viruses are typically self-limiting skin lesions, not fatal systemic disease.
  • Transmission occurs through direct contact with infected animals or lesions, not primarily via mosquito bites.
Know More
  • Protective gloves and good hygiene practices reduce occupational zoonotic risk.
  • Human lesions typically resolve without specific antiviral treatment.
  • Immunocompromised individuals may experience more severe or prolonged infections.
  • Awareness among veterinary and farming personnel aids early recognition and prevention.

posts.post_title: Genus and family of African swine fever virus
posts.post_content: African swine fever virus (ASFV) belongs to which genus and family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Genus Asfivirus, family Asfarviridae

ASFV belongs to genus Asfivirus, the sole member of family Asfarviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

It is unique among DNA arboviruses infecting mammals, and is the only DNA virus transmitted by Ornithodoros soft ticks.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pestivirus/Flaviviridae covers classical swine fever virus, an RNA virus clinically similar but taxonomically completely different.
  • Orthopoxvirus/Poxviridae covers cowpox and vaccinia viruses, unrelated to ASFV.
  • Orbivirus/Reoviridae covers bluetongue and AHS viruses, unrelated to ASFV.
Know More
  • ASFV is a large, complex, enveloped DNA virus.
  • Mortality can approach 100% with highly virulent strains.
  • OIE Listing: List A disease.
  • No effective vaccine is currently widely available; control relies on stamping out and biosecurity.

posts.post_title: Biological vector of African swine fever virus
posts.post_content: Which arthropod acts as a biological vector for African swine fever virus, unlike vectors of most other veterinary viral diseases?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ornithodoros soft ticks

Ornithodoros soft ticks act as a true biological vector, in which the virus can also replicate.

Correct Option Explanation

This makes ASFV unique as a DNA virus with an arthropod-borne (arbovirus) transmission cycle, alongside direct contact and fomite-based spread.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Culicoides midges transmit bluetongue and African horse sickness viruses, not ASFV.
  • Anopheles mosquitoes are not the documented vector for ASFV.
  • Ixodes hard ticks are not the vector associated with ASFV; the soft tick genus Ornithodoros is specifically implicated.
Know More
  • Wild African suids (warthogs, bushpigs) serve as reservoir hosts along with the tick vector.
  • Direct contact and contaminated feed/fomites are also important transmission routes, especially in domestic pigs.
  • Clinical signs include high fever, cyanosis, and haemorrhages.
  • Genetic diversity among ASFV strains (genotypes) complicates control efforts.

posts.post_title: Wildlife reservoir of African swine fever virus
posts.post_content: Which wild suid species serves as an important natural reservoir of African swine fever virus in Africa, along with the tick vector?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Warthogs

Warthogs (and bushpigs) serve as important wildlife reservoirs of ASFV in Africa.

Correct Option Explanation

Warthogs are usually subclinically infected, maintaining a sylvatic cycle with Ornithodoros ticks that can spill over to domestic pigs when contact occurs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Zebras serve as a reservoir for African horse sickness virus, not ASFV.
  • Elephants are not a documented ASFV reservoir host.
  • Buffaloes are important reservoirs of FMD virus in Africa, not ASFV.
Know More
  • The sylvatic (wild) cycle differs from the domestic cycle, which relies more on direct pig-to-pig contact.
  • Domestic pig outbreaks can cause devastating mortality and economic loss.
  • Diagnosis includes virus isolation, PCR, and antigen/antibody detection tests.
  • Global spread has occurred through movement of infected pigs, pork products, and contaminated fomites.

posts.post_title: Structural feature distinguishing ASFV from other veterinary DNA viruses
posts.post_content: African swine fever virus is notable for being the only DNA virus among common livestock pathogens that behaves as what?

_aimcq_options.text: A virus with a segmented genome
A virus with no capsid at all

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A tick-borne arbovirus

ASFV is notable as the only DNA virus in this course that behaves as a tick-borne arbovirus.

Correct Option Explanation

This is because it can replicate within its Ornithodoros soft tick vector, a property typically associated with certain RNA arboviruses rather than DNA viruses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • ASFV is actually enveloped, not non-enveloped.
  • ASFV has a single, large, linear double-stranded DNA genome, not a segmented one.
  • ASFV has a well-defined icosahedral capsid, so 'no capsid at all' is incorrect.
Know More
  • ASFV genome size is one of the largest among animal DNA viruses.
  • The virus encodes many proteins involved in immune evasion within host cells.
  • ASF has no zoonotic potential; it does not infect humans.
  • Strict import controls on pork products help prevent introduction into ASF-free countries.

posts.post_title: Primary control strategy for African swine fever outbreaks
posts.post_content: In the absence of a widely available effective vaccine, what is the primary strategy used to control African swine fever outbreaks in domestic pigs?

_aimcq_options.text: Stamping out (culling) and strict biosecurity/movement control
Mass antibiotic treatment of all pigs
Widespread use of a licensed inactivated vaccine

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Stamping out (culling) and strict biosecurity/movement control

Stamping out and strict biosecurity/movement control are the primary control strategies.

Correct Option Explanation

Since a broadly effective, widely licensed vaccine has historically not been available, rapid culling of affected and in-contact herds, along with quarantine and movement restrictions, remains central to outbreak control.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Antibiotics have no effect on this viral disease.
  • Antiparasitic drenching does not address the tick-borne and direct-contact transmission routes relevant to ASF control.
  • A widely licensed, broadly effective vaccine has not historically been available, though research vaccines are in development.
Know More
  • Disinfection of premises and equipment is critical after an outbreak.
  • Wild boar populations can also maintain and spread the virus in some regions.
  • Trade restrictions on pigs and pork products help prevent international spread.
  • Early detection and reporting are essential given the severity and rapid spread potential of ASF.

posts.post_title: Clinical presentation of highly virulent African swine fever strains
posts.post_content: Highly virulent strains of African swine fever virus typically cause which clinical picture in domestic pigs?

_aimcq_options.text: High fever, cyanosis, and haemorrhages with very high mortality
Chronic, painless skin nodules with full recovery
Purely respiratory disease with no systemic signs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: High fever, cyanosis, and haemorrhages with very high mortality

Highly virulent ASFV strains cause high fever, cyanosis, and haemorrhages, often with mortality approaching 100%.

Correct Option Explanation

This severe, often peracute-to-acute clinical picture, involving multiple organ systems, is a hallmark of highly virulent strain infections, distinguishing ASF from milder chronic strains that can occur with less virulent variants.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Chronic, painless skin nodules with full recovery describes a much milder pattern seen with some low-virulence strains, not the classic highly virulent presentation.
  • Mild, self-limiting diarrhoea does not capture the severe, systemic nature of highly virulent ASF.
  • ASF is a systemic disease with multiple organ involvement, not purely respiratory.
Know More
  • Post-mortem findings often include an enlarged, friable spleen and widespread haemorrhages.
  • Less virulent strains can cause more chronic, less predictable clinical courses.
  • Differential diagnosis from classical swine fever requires laboratory confirmation.
  • Rapid diagnosis and reporting are critical given the disease's severity and spread potential.

posts.post_title: Family and synonym of pseudorabies virus
posts.post_content: Pseudorabies virus, also known as Aujeszky's disease virus, belongs to which family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Herpesviridae

Pseudorabies virus belongs to family Herpesviridae, subfamily Alphaherpesvirinae.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes Aujeszky's disease primarily in pigs, the natural reservoir host, but can cause fatal disease in many other mammals that come into contact with infected pigs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Poxviridae covers viruses like swine pox and vaccinia, structurally very different, larger DNA viruses.
  • Rhabdoviridae covers rabies virus, an unrelated bullet-shaped RNA virus family.
  • Flaviviridae covers CSF and BVD viruses, RNA viruses unrelated to pseudorabies virus.
Know More
  • Pigs are the natural reservoir and generally survive infection.
  • Other species (cattle, dogs, cats) usually die once infected, showing intense itching ('mad itch').
  • Like other herpesviruses, it can establish lifelong latent infection.
  • Eradication programs in pigs rely on marker vaccines and serological testing.

posts.post_title: Natural reservoir host of pseudorabies virus
posts.post_content: Which species is the natural reservoir host of pseudorabies (Aujeszky's disease) virus, generally surviving infection?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pigs

Pigs are the natural reservoir host, generally surviving infection, especially as adults.

Correct Option Explanation

Young piglets can suffer high mortality, but adult pigs often survive with mild or subclinical disease and can become latently infected carriers.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Cattle are 'dead-end', highly susceptible hosts that usually die once infected, not the natural reservoir.
  • Dogs similarly usually die once infected, unlike the reservoir species.
  • Cats also typically succumb to fatal disease if infected, not serving as the reservoir host.
Know More
  • Non-reservoir species often show intense pruritus, called 'mad itch', before death.
  • Transmission is mainly via direct contact, respiratory secretions, and contaminated feed.
  • Latency in the trigeminal ganglia is a key feature of pig infection.
  • Eradication programs have successfully eliminated the disease from commercial pig populations in several countries.

posts.post_title: Characteristic clinical sign in non-reservoir hosts infected with pseudorabies virus
posts.post_content: In cattle, dogs, and cats infected with pseudorabies virus, a characteristic and intense clinical sign, giving rise to the common name 'mad itch', is what?

_aimcq_options.text: Complete loss of appetite with no other signs
Painless swelling of the joints only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Severe, intense pruritus (itching)

Severe, intense pruritus (itching) is the hallmark sign, giving rise to the name 'mad itch'.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected animals often self-mutilate by scratching and biting at the affected area, and the disease is invariably fatal in these non-reservoir species, usually within 1-2 days of sign onset.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Appetite loss alone does not capture the specific, dramatic pruritic sign associated with this disease.
  • Painless joint swelling is not the characteristic sign of pseudorabies in these species.
  • Progressive blindness is not the hallmark sign; instead, intense itching with neurological involvement is typical.
Know More
  • Death typically follows rapidly once neurological signs and severe pruritus appear.
  • Diagnosis includes virus isolation, PCR, and histopathology showing characteristic herpesvirus inclusions.
  • Prevention in non-pig species centres on avoiding contact with infected pigs or contaminated material.
  • No effective treatment exists once clinical signs develop in these susceptible species.

posts.post_title: Latency site of pseudorabies virus in pigs
posts.post_content: Similar to other alphaherpesviruses, pseudorabies virus establishes latency in pigs primarily in which anatomical site?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Trigeminal ganglia (sensory nerve ganglia)

Pseudorabies virus establishes latency in the trigeminal ganglia, similar to other alphaherpesviruses.

Correct Option Explanation

This latent infection can reactivate under stress, leading to intermittent shedding and ongoing risk of transmission from apparently healthy carrier pigs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bone marrow is not the primary latency site for alphaherpesviruses like this one.
  • Skeletal muscle fibres are not the documented latency site for pseudorabies virus.
  • Red blood cells lack a nucleus and cannot support herpesvirus latency.
Know More
  • Latently infected pigs can reactivate and shed virus during periods of stress.
  • Serological testing (ELISA) helps identify latently infected carrier animals.
  • Marker (gene-deleted) vaccines allow differentiation of vaccinated from infected pigs.
  • Many countries have successfully eradicated Aujeszky's disease from commercial herds.

posts.post_title: Family and cell type affected in Marek's disease
posts.post_content: Marek's disease virus, a herpesvirus causing lymphoproliferative disease in chickens, primarily transforms which cell type?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: T-lymphocytes

Marek's disease virus primarily transforms T-lymphocytes, leading to malignant lymphoma formation.

Correct Option Explanation

This oncogenic (tumour-causing) property distinguishes Marek's disease virus from most other herpesviruses in veterinary medicine, and the resulting lymphomas can infiltrate peripheral nerves and visceral organs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Erythrocytes lack the nuclear machinery required for viral transformation and are not the target cell.
  • Hepatocytes may show secondary tumour infiltration but are not the primary transformed cell type.
  • Skeletal myocytes are not the primary cell type transformed by Marek's disease virus.
Know More
  • Marek's disease virus belongs to family Herpesviridae, subfamily Alphaherpesvirinae.
  • Peripheral nerve enlargement causes characteristic paralysis ('range paralysis').
  • Herpesvirus of turkeys (HVT) is used as a related, non-oncogenic vaccine virus.
  • Vaccination at the hatchery is a cornerstone of Marek's disease control.

posts.post_title: Characteristic clinical sign of Marek's disease due to peripheral nerve involvement
posts.post_content: Enlargement of peripheral nerves due to lymphomatous infiltration in Marek's disease commonly causes what characteristic clinical presentation in affected chickens?

_aimcq_options.text: Sudden death with no premonitory signs in every case
Complete blindness with no locomotor signs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Range paralysis (leg and wing paralysis)

Peripheral nerve involvement classically causes range paralysis, affecting the legs and wings.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected birds may show a characteristic splayed-leg posture (one leg forward, one back) due to asymmetric nerve involvement, along with visceral lymphomas in severe cases.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Profuse watery diarrhoea is not the characteristic sign; the disease is primarily neurological and lymphoproliferative.
  • Sudden death without premonitory signs can occur with visceral tumours but is not the classic 'characteristic' presentation described here.
  • Ocular lesions can occur in some cases (grey eye), but complete blindness with no locomotor signs misrepresents the classic presentation.
Know More
  • Ocular form ('grey eye' or iris discolouration) can also occur.
  • Visceral lymphomas can involve the liver, spleen, gonads, and other organs.
  • Vaccination has dramatically reduced Marek's disease losses in commercial poultry.
  • The disease has both an early acute cytolytic phase and a later lymphomatous phase.

posts.post_title: Vaccine virus used to protect against Marek's disease
posts.post_content: Which related, non-oncogenic herpesvirus is commonly used as a vaccine to protect chickens against Marek's disease?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Herpesvirus of turkeys (HVT)

Herpesvirus of turkeys (HVT) is commonly used as a vaccine virus against Marek's disease.

Correct Option Explanation

HVT is antigenically related to Marek's disease virus but is non-oncogenic in chickens, making it an effective and safe vaccine strain, often given at the hatchery on day of hatch.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pseudorabies virus is a swine pathogen, unrelated to Marek's disease vaccination in chickens.
  • Infectious laryngotracheitis virus is a distinct herpesvirus causing a different respiratory disease of chickens, not used as a Marek's vaccine.
  • Duck plague virus is a herpesvirus of ducks, unrelated to Marek's disease vaccination.
Know More
  • Vaccination is typically given via in ovo injection or at day-old in the hatchery.
  • Vaccination prevents clinical disease and tumour formation but does not always prevent infection.
  • Genetically resistant chicken lines have also been developed through selective breeding.
  • Marek's disease vaccination is considered one of the first successful anti-cancer vaccines in any species.

posts.post_title: Family classification of egg drop syndrome virus
posts.post_content: Egg drop syndrome (EDS) virus, causing a sudden decline in egg production and shell quality in layers, belongs to which family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Adenoviridae

EDS virus belongs to family Adenoviridae, genus Atadenovirus.

Correct Option Explanation

It causes soft-shelled, thin-shelled, or shell-less eggs, along with a marked drop in egg production, without significant mortality or respiratory signs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Coronaviridae covers infectious bronchitis virus, which can also affect egg quality but via a different mechanism and family.
  • Paramyxoviridae covers Newcastle disease virus, unrelated to EDS.
  • Reoviridae covers bluetongue and related viruses, unrelated to EDS.
Know More
  • EDS was originally linked to a duck adenovirus that crossed into chickens via contaminated vaccine.
  • Egg production may drop by 10-40% during an outbreak.
  • Diagnosis uses haemagglutination and haemagglutination inhibition tests, since the virus agglutinates certain RBCs.
  • Vaccination with inactivated vaccine is used preventively before onset of lay.

posts.post_title: Characteristic egg abnormality in egg drop syndrome
posts.post_content: Which egg quality abnormality is most characteristic of egg drop syndrome in affected laying flocks?

_aimcq_options.text: Eggs with unusually thick, hardened shells
Eggs that are consistently larger than normal

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Soft-shelled, thin-shelled, or shell-less eggs

Egg drop syndrome causes soft-shelled, thin-shelled, or shell-less eggs.

Correct Option Explanation

This reflects the virus's damaging effect on the shell gland region of the oviduct, occurring alongside a general decline in egg output, without notable mortality or overt respiratory disease.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Thicker, hardened shells are the opposite of the actual shell defect seen with this disease.
  • Double-yolked eggs are not the characteristic abnormality associated with EDS.
  • Eggs are not consistently larger; shell and production defects, not size increase, are the hallmark.
Know More
  • Pigmentation loss in brown-shelled eggs can also occur during outbreaks.
  • The disease usually causes minimal impact on bird health otherwise.
  • Vertical (egg-transmitted) and horizontal spread both contribute to disease persistence.
  • Good biosecurity and vaccination help minimise flock-level losses.

posts.post_title: Original source implicated in the emergence of egg drop syndrome
posts.post_content: Egg drop syndrome virus was originally believed to have crossed into commercial chicken flocks from which source?

_aimcq_options.text: A duck adenovirus, via contaminated vaccine
A fungal contaminant in poultry feed

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A duck adenovirus, via contaminated vaccine

EDS virus was originally linked to a duck adenovirus that entered chicken flocks via contaminated vaccine material.

Correct Option Explanation

This historical origin explains why waterfowl remain natural hosts of related adenoviruses, and why vaccine production quality control is important to prevent similar cross-species introductions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • EDS virus is not documented as mosquito-borne; it spreads mainly horizontally and vertically among birds.
  • EDS is caused by a virus (adenovirus), not a bacterial pathogen.
  • A fungal contaminant is not implicated in the origin of EDS virus.
Know More
  • Waterfowl, including ducks and geese, can be natural, often subclinical, hosts of related adenoviruses.
  • Serological surveillance helps detect subclinical circulation in flocks.
  • Inactivated vaccines given before the onset of lay are the mainstay of prevention.
  • Outbreaks tend to occur in flocks around peak production age.

posts.post_title: Family and common name of infectious canine hepatitis virus
posts.post_content: Infectious canine hepatitis (ICH), also known as Rubarth's disease, is caused by a virus of which family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Adenoviridae

ICH is caused by canine adenovirus type 1 (CAV-1), family Adenoviridae.

Correct Option Explanation

It primarily targets the liver and vascular endothelium, producing hepatitis and vasculitis, and can cause the characteristic 'blue eye' (corneal oedema) as a post-recovery complication.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Parvoviridae includes canine parvovirus, which causes enteritis/myocarditis, a different disease from ICH.
  • Herpesviridae includes canine herpesvirus, which causes a different, mainly neonatal disease.
  • Circoviridae includes chicken anaemia virus, unrelated to ICH.
Know More
  • Synonym: Rubarth's disease.
  • Vaccination commonly uses the related, non-hepatotropic CAV-2 strain to avoid vaccine-induced blue eye.
  • Severe cases show hepatic necrosis, jaundice, and haemorrhagic tendencies.
  • Recovered dogs may shed virus in urine for extended periods.

posts.post_title: Post-recovery ocular complication of infectious canine hepatitis
posts.post_content: Dogs recovering from infectious canine hepatitis may develop a characteristic ocular complication known as what?

_aimcq_options.text: Complete and permanent blindness in all cases
Retinal detachment with no corneal involvement

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 'Blue eye' (corneal oedema)

'Blue eye', or corneal oedema, is a characteristic post-recovery complication of ICH.

Correct Option Explanation

This immune complex-mediated reaction causes a bluish clouding of the cornea, typically appearing days after recovery, and it usually resolves without permanent visual impairment.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complete and permanent blindness in all cases overstates the outcome; blue eye is usually transient and self-limiting.
  • Cataracts present at birth are not the documented complication linked to ICH.
  • The condition specifically involves the cornea (blue eye), not primarily retinal detachment.
Know More
  • Blue eye is thought to result from an antigen-antibody immune complex reaction in the cornea.
  • The related CAV-2 vaccine strain is preferred because it is less likely to cause this ocular reaction.
  • ICH can also cause interstitial nephritis in some recovering dogs.
  • Vaccination has greatly reduced the incidence of clinical ICH in vaccinated dog populations.

posts.post_title: Vaccine strain preferred for protecting dogs against infectious canine hepatitis
posts.post_content: To avoid vaccine-induced 'blue eye', vaccination against infectious canine hepatitis commonly uses which related virus strain instead of CAV-1?

_aimcq_options.text: Rockborn strain of canine distemper virus

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Canine adenovirus type 2 (CAV-2)

CAV-2, which primarily causes respiratory disease, is used as a safer vaccine strain against ICH.

Correct Option Explanation

CAV-2 shares protective cross-reactive antigens with CAV-1 but is far less likely to cause the corneal oedema ('blue eye') reaction associated with CAV-1-based vaccines.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Canine parvovirus type 2b is used for parvoviral enteritis vaccination, a different disease from ICH.
  • The Rockborn strain is used for canine distemper vaccination, not ICH.
  • The Flury strain is a rabies vaccine strain, unrelated to ICH.
Know More
  • CAV-2 is also a component of combination ('DHPP'-type) vaccines for dogs.
  • Modern multivalent vaccines typically protect against distemper, hepatitis, parvovirus and parainfluenza together.
  • Puppies are especially vulnerable to severe, sometimes fulminant, ICH.
  • Good vaccination coverage has made severe clinical ICH relatively uncommon in well-vaccinated populations.

posts.post_title: Family classification of canine parvovirus
posts.post_content: Canine parvovirus (CPV-2), a major cause of viral enteritis in dogs, belongs to which family?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Parvoviridae

Canine parvovirus belongs to family Parvoviridae, one of the smallest known animal DNA viruses.

Correct Option Explanation

CPV-2 emerged in the late 1970s, likely as a variant of feline panleukopenia virus, and rapidly spread worldwide causing severe enteritis and myocarditis in dogs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Adenoviridae includes infectious canine hepatitis virus, a different, larger DNA virus family.
  • Circoviridae includes chicken anaemia virus, a distinct small DNA virus family.
  • Papillomaviridae includes wart-causing papillomaviruses, unrelated to CPV.
Know More
  • CPV targets rapidly dividing cells, especially intestinal crypt epithelium and bone marrow.
  • Puppies can also develop fatal myocarditis if infected in utero or very early in life.
  • The virus is extremely stable in the environment, resisting many disinfectants.
  • Vaccination is highly effective and forms a core part of puppy vaccination schedules.

posts.post_title: Tissue tropism of canine parvovirus explaining its clinical effects
posts.post_content: Canine parvovirus preferentially infects which type of cells, explaining its severe effects on the intestine and, in young puppies, the heart?

_aimcq_options.text: Rapidly dividing cells, such as intestinal crypt epithelium and myocardial cells in neonates

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rapidly dividing cells, such as intestinal crypt epithelium and myocardial cells in neonates

CPV preferentially infects rapidly dividing cells, explaining its intestinal and, in neonates, cardiac effects.

Correct Option Explanation

Because the virus requires actively dividing host cells to replicate, it targets tissues with high mitotic activity: intestinal crypt cells in dogs of any age, and myocardial cells specifically in very young, still-developing puppies.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Mature, non-dividing neurons are not the primary target, as they lack the active cell division CPV requires for replication.
  • Mature red blood cells are anucleate and cannot support any viral replication.

posts.post_title: Environmental stability of canine parvovirus

posts.post_title: Relationship between canine parvovirus and feline panleukopenia virus

posts.post_title: Cause of profound leukopenia in parvoviral infections

posts.post_title: Family classification of bovine and canine papillomaviruses

posts.post_title: Typical clinical course of bovine papillomas

posts.post_title: Family and immune target of chicken anaemia virus

posts.post_title: Nature of the infectious agent causing bovine spongiform encephalopathy

posts.post_title: Source implicated in the emergence of bovine spongiform encephalopathy

posts.post_title: Number of structural proteins in Newcastle disease virus

posts.post_title: Molecular basis of Newcastle disease virus virulence

posts.post_title: Phenomenon underlying emergence of novel influenza strains
