  • Virus enters host cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis (pinocytosis through clathrin-coated pits).
  • The N protein encapsidates the genomic RNA, forming the ribonucleoprotein complex with P and L.
  • Vaccine efficacy is largely dependent on generating strong antibody responses against the G protein.

posts.post_title: Rabies virus target region within the brain
posts.post_content: Rabies virus tends to be most abundant in which regions of the brain during clinical infection?

_aimcq_options.text: Cerebellar cortex exclusively, with no brainstem involvement

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Thalamus, pons, and medulla

Rabies virus is most abundant in the thalamus, pons, and medulla.

Correct Option Explanation

These are key brainstem and diencephalic structures, and their involvement correlates with the severe autonomic and behavioural disturbances seen in clinical rabies, including the classic furious and paralytic presentations.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • While the cerebellum (notably Purkinje cells) is also involved, exclusive cerebellar involvement without brainstem changes does not match the described distribution.
  • The occipital lobe alone is not the primary site of viral concentration described.
  • The corpus callosum alone is not the primary site of viral concentration described.
Know More
  • Negri bodies are especially frequent in the pyramidal cells of Ammon's horn (hippocampus) and cerebellar Purkinje cells.
  • Direct fluorescent antibody testing on fresh brain tissue remains the gold-standard diagnostic method.
  • The virus spreads centripetally along peripheral nerves toward the CNS following a bite.
  • Once clinical signs appear, rabies is essentially always fatal.

posts.post_title: Purpose of post-exposure passive immunization in rabies
posts.post_content: In post-exposure rabies prophylaxis, rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is administered around the wound site primarily to achieve what?

_aimcq_options.text: Provide immediate passive antibody protection while active immunity develops from vaccination
Replace the need for wound washing entirely
Permanently cure clinical rabies once symptoms begin
Prevent any future need for vaccination in that person

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Provide immediate passive antibody protection while active immunity develops from vaccination

RIG provides immediate passive antibody protection at the wound site, bridging the gap until active immunity develops from vaccination.

Correct Option Explanation

Since vaccine-induced active immunity takes time to develop, RIG neutralises virus at the bite site right away, and is typically infiltrated directly around the wound according to current post-exposure protocols.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Thorough wound washing with soap and water remains an essential separate step and is not replaced by RIG administration.
  • RIG is a preventive, pre-symptomatic intervention; it cannot cure clinical rabies once symptoms have begun, as the disease is then essentially always fatal.
  • RIG does not eliminate the need for the accompanying vaccine series; both are given together in appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis.
Know More
  • Both human rabies immunoglobulin (HRIG) and equine rabies immunoglobulin (ERIG) are used, with ERIG being more affordable.
  • Prompt, thorough wound washing with soap and water is one of the most effective early interventions.
  • Post-exposure vaccination typically follows a multi-dose schedule given in the deltoid muscle.
  • Early, complete post-exposure prophylaxis is essentially 100% effective in preventing clinical rabies.

posts.post_title: Milk yield impact during bovine ephemeral fever
posts.post_content: During the acute febrile phase of bovine ephemeral fever, lactating cows typically show what change in milk production?

_aimcq_options.text: A sharp drop in milk production
A permanent, lifelong increase in milk yield
No change whatsoever in milk yield
Immediate, complete cessation of lactation forever

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A sharp drop in milk production

A sharp drop in milk production occurs during the acute febrile phase.

Correct Option Explanation

This reflects the systemic impact of high fever and general malaise typical of BEF; milk yield usually recovers once the animal passes through the short, self-limiting clinical course.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A permanent increase in milk yield is the opposite of the documented, temporary decline.
  • 'No change whatsoever' contradicts the well-documented productivity impact of the febrile illness.
  • Permanent cessation of lactation is an overstatement; most cows recover normal milk production after the brief illness resolves.
Know More
  • Recovery is typically rapid, within about 72 hours, matching the 'three-day sickness' name.
  • Well-conditioned, high-producing dairy cattle tend to show more pronounced clinical signs.
  • Secondary complications like downer cow syndrome can occasionally occur in severe cases.
  • No specific antiviral treatment exists; supportive care (anti-inflammatories, fluids) aids recovery.

posts.post_title: Complication of severe bovine ephemeral fever in heavy cattle
posts.post_content: In severe cases of bovine ephemeral fever, particularly in large, heavily-muscled cattle, which complication related to prolonged recumbency can occur?

_aimcq_options.text: Congenital limb deformity in the affected animal itself

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Downer cow syndrome

Severe BEF cases, especially in large cattle, can occasionally progress to downer cow syndrome.

Correct Option Explanation

Prolonged recumbency and muscle/joint pain from the acute illness can lead to secondary complications such as pressure-related muscle damage, making it harder for heavy animals to rise again even after the primary fever resolves.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Congenital limb deformity refers to a birth defect, not a complication of an acute adult-onset febrile illness like BEF.
  • Permanent blindness is not a documented complication of BEF.
  • Complete loss of hearing is not a documented complication of BEF.
Know More
  • Supportive nursing care, including assistance to stand, can help prevent this complication.
  • Most cattle recover fully without long-term complications if managed appropriately.
  • The disease's economic impact often comes more from lost productivity than from mortality.
  • Vaccination is available in some endemic regions to reduce outbreak severity.

posts.post_title: Basis for FMD serotype-specific vaccine matching
posts.post_content: Why is antigenic matching between the vaccine strain and the circulating field strain particularly critical for foot-and-mouth disease vaccination?

_aimcq_options.text: Because there is no cross-protection between the seven FMD serotypes
Because FMD virus is a DNA virus with a stable genome
Because only one FMD serotype has ever existed
Because FMD vaccines never require matching to field strains

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Because there is no cross-protection between the seven FMD serotypes

Antigenic matching is critical because there is no cross-protection between the seven FMD serotypes (and limited cross-protection even between subtypes).

Correct Option Explanation

This means a vaccine effective against serotype O, for example, will not protect against serotype A or Asia1, so ongoing surveillance and vaccine strain selection matched to circulating field strains is essential for effective control.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • FMD virus is an RNA virus, not DNA, and its genome is notably prone to mutation, not stable.
  • FMD virus specifically has seven serotypes, not just one.
  • FMD vaccines specifically do require careful strain matching due to the lack of cross-protection, contrary to this option.
Know More
  • Vaccine matching studies (vaccine matching tests) help predict field vaccine efficacy against circulating strains.
  • Regional reference laboratories track circulating FMD serotypes and subtypes.
  • Inactivated whole-virus vaccines remain the standard vaccine type for FMD control.
  • Ring vaccination around outbreak zones is a common control strategy in endemic regions.

posts.post_title: Role of pigs in foot-and-mouth disease epidemiology
posts.post_content: Pigs are often described as 'amplifier' hosts for foot-and-mouth disease virus because of what characteristic?

_aimcq_options.text: They shed large amounts of aerosolised virus, contributing to airborne spread
They are completely resistant to infection
They only transmit the virus through vertical (in utero) infection
They never develop clinical vesicular lesions

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: They shed large amounts of aerosolised virus, contributing to airborne spread

Pigs shed particularly large amounts of aerosolised virus, earning them the description of 'amplifier' hosts.

Correct Option Explanation

This high-volume aerosol shedding can contribute significantly to airborne spread of FMD virus over considerable distances, especially under favourable weather conditions, making pig populations a key epidemiological concern during outbreaks.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Pigs are actually highly susceptible to FMD, not resistant, and develop clinical vesicular disease.
  • Pigs transmit FMD primarily via aerosol and direct/indirect contact, not solely via vertical transmission.
  • Pigs do develop clinical vesicular lesions on the feet and snout, unlike this incorrect claim.
Know More
  • Ruminants like cattle and sheep can become long-term subclinical carriers, unlike pigs.
  • Wind-borne spread of FMD virus from infected pig premises has been documented over long distances under the right conditions.
  • Understanding species-specific transmission dynamics informs targeted control measures during outbreaks.
  • Movement restrictions on pigs are often particularly strict during FMD outbreaks for this reason.

posts.post_title: Duration of the FMD carrier state in cattle
posts.post_content: Recovered cattle can remain subclinical carriers of foot-and-mouth disease virus for up to approximately how long?

_aimcq_options.text: Never; cattle cannot become FMD carriers

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3.5 years

Recovered cattle can remain FMD carriers for up to approximately 3.5 years.

Correct Option Explanation

This prolonged carrier state, detected using probang (oesophageal-pharyngeal) sampling, is a major complicating factor for FMD eradication programs, since carriers can potentially contribute to disease persistence even without showing clinical signs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 3.5 days and 3.5 weeks substantially understate the documented duration of the carrier state in cattle.
  • Cattle are, in fact, well documented to become long-term carriers, contradicting 'never'.
Know More
  • Buffaloes and sheep can also become carriers, though the epidemiological significance of the carrier state is still debated.
  • Carrier detection relies on specialised probang sampling and virus isolation or PCR testing.
  • FMD-free countries maintain strict import controls partly to prevent introduction of carrier animals.
  • The carrier phenomenon does not occur with all FMD serotypes to the same extent.

posts.post_title: Route of introduction of FMD virus onto naive farms
posts.post_content: Which of the following is a well-documented route by which foot-and-mouth disease virus can be introduced onto a previously unaffected farm?

_aimcq_options.text: Introduction of infected animals or contaminated animal products
Exposure to sunlight alone, without any animal or product contact
Consumption of properly cooked meat only
Contact with fully inactivated vaccine only

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Introduction of infected animals or contaminated animal products

Introduction of infected animals or contaminated animal products (meat, milk, hides) is a well-documented route of FMD introduction.

Correct Option Explanation

Airborne spread, contaminated vehicles/equipment, and human movement between farms are also important routes, making biosecurity a central pillar of FMD prevention.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Sunlight exposure alone, without any animal or product contact, is not a documented introduction route; in fact, FMD virus is relatively sensitive to UV light and drying.
  • Properly cooked meat is generally considered safe, since adequate cooking inactivates FMD virus, unlike raw or undercooked contaminated products.
  • Properly inactivated vaccine, by definition, does not contain infectious virus and would not introduce disease.
Know More
  • Vehicles, footwear, and clothing can mechanically carry virus between premises if not properly disinfected.
  • Quarantine of new arrivals and thorough biosecurity protocols reduce introduction risk.
  • Wildlife species susceptible to FMD can also play a role in some regional epidemiology.
  • Rapid reporting and response are critical once an incursion is suspected.

posts.post_title: Immunotolerance mechanism in classical swine fever carrier piglets
posts.post_content: Piglets persistently infected in utero with classical swine fever virus become immunotolerant, meaning what happens to their immune response?

_aimcq_options.text: Their immune system recognises the virus as 'self' and fails to mount a protective response
They mount an unusually strong, protective antibody response that clears the virus quickly
They become completely resistant to all future viral infections
Their immune system is entirely absent from birth

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Their immune system recognises the virus as 'self' and fails to mount a protective response

Immunotolerant piglets fail to recognise CSF virus as foreign, treating it as 'self', so they mount no effective protective immune response.

Correct Option Explanation

This occurs because exposure happens during a critical window of fetal immune development, before the immune system has learned to distinguish self from non-self, allowing lifelong persistent, silent infection and continuous viral shedding.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • These piglets specifically fail to mount a strong protective response — that is the defining feature of immunotolerance, the opposite of this option.
  • Immunotolerant piglets are not broadly resistant to other infections; the tolerance is specific to CSF virus.
  • These piglets have a functioning immune system generally; it is specifically tolerant to CSF virus antigens, not absent altogether.
Know More
  • A similar immunotolerance mechanism occurs with BVDV persistent infection in cattle.
  • Immunotolerant piglets may appear normal or show poor growth ('runting') and congenital tremor.
  • These carrier piglets are epidemiologically important as a continuous source of virus for the herd.
  • Identifying and removing such carriers is central to CSF control and eradication programs.

posts.post_title: Live vaccine strain used to control classical swine fever
posts.post_content: Which live attenuated vaccine strain is widely used for classical swine fever control, providing strong protective immunity?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: The Chinese (C) strain

The Chinese (C) strain is a widely used live attenuated vaccine for CSF, providing strong, durable protective immunity.

Correct Option Explanation

It has been used effectively for decades in many endemic countries, though newer marker vaccines are increasingly used where differentiation of infected from vaccinated animals is required for eradication programs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • The La Sota strain is a Newcastle disease vaccine strain, unrelated to CSF.
  • The Rockborn strain is a canine distemper vaccine strain, unrelated to CSF.
  • The TC-83 strain is a Venezuelan equine encephalomyelitis vaccine strain, unrelated to CSF.
Know More
  • Marker vaccines allow serological differentiation of vaccinated from naturally infected pigs (DIVA strategy).
  • CSF-free countries typically prohibit vaccination and rely on strict import controls and surveillance instead.
  • Vaccination is a key tool in endemic regions where eradication is not immediately feasible.
  • Combined vaccination and culling strategies have successfully eliminated CSF from several regions.

posts.post_title: Skin manifestation of acute classical swine fever
posts.post_content: Acute classical swine fever commonly causes what visible change to the skin of affected pigs?

_aimcq_options.text: Purplish discolouration from haemorrhages, especially on ears, snout, and abdomen
Complete, uniform whitening of the entire skin surface
Development of wool-like hair growth over the whole body
No skin changes are ever seen in this disease

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Purplish discolouration from haemorrhages, especially on ears, snout, and abdomen

Acute CSF causes purplish skin discolouration from haemorrhages, especially on the ears, snout, and abdomen.

Correct Option Explanation

This haemorrhagic diathesis reflects widespread vascular damage caused by the virus, and is a classic, though not universally present, clinical clue used alongside fever and other systemic signs in suspecting CSF.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Uniform skin whitening is not a documented feature of CSF; the characteristic change is purplish discolouration, not whitening.
  • Wool-like hair growth is not a documented feature of this disease.
  • Skin changes are, in fact, a recognised and diagnostically useful feature in many acute CSF cases, so 'no skin changes' is incorrect.
Know More
  • Other clinical signs include high fever, conjunctivitis, and neurological disturbances in some cases.
  • Chronic cases can show intestinal button ulcers and prolonged wasting.
  • Differential diagnosis includes African swine fever, which can appear clinically very similar.
  • Laboratory confirmation is essential to distinguish CSF from other haemorrhagic swine diseases.

posts.post_title: Global eradication status comparison of classical swine fever
posts.post_content: Regarding the global distribution of classical swine fever, which statement is most accurate?

_aimcq_options.text: It has been eradicated from North America and much of Europe, but remains endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, and Central/South America
It has never existed anywhere in the world
It is equally endemic in every country worldwide with no eradication successes
It was eradicated everywhere on earth by the 1950s

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: It has been eradicated from North America and much of Europe, but remains endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, and Central/South America

CSF has been eradicated from North America and much of Europe, but remains endemic in parts of Asia, Africa, and Central/South America.

Correct Option Explanation

This mixed global picture reflects varying levels of investment in surveillance, vaccination, and biosecurity across different regions and illustrates ongoing global animal health challenges.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • CSF is a well-documented, historically significant disease, so 'never existed anywhere' is factually incorrect.
  • Distribution is uneven, with successful eradication in some regions, contradicting 'equally endemic everywhere with no successes'.
  • CSF was not eradicated everywhere by the 1950s; it remains endemic in various regions even in more recent decades.
Know More
  • Ongoing risk of reintroduction into CSF-free areas necessitates continued surveillance and import controls.
  • Wild boar populations can complicate eradication in some parts of Europe and Asia.
  • Regional and international collaboration supports control programs in endemic areas.
  • Rapid response protocols are essential to prevent re-establishment in previously CSF-free regions.

posts.post_title: Congenital defect classically linked to fetal BVDV infection
posts.post_content: Mid-gestation fetal infection with BVDV is classically associated with which congenital neurological defect in calves?

_aimcq_options.text: Complete absence of the brain (anencephaly) in every case
Permanent, universal deafness with no other signs
Extra limbs (polymelia) in every affected calf

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cerebellar hypoplasia

Cerebellar hypoplasia is the classic congenital defect linked to mid-gestation fetal BVDV infection.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected calves typically show ataxia, incoordination, and a wide-based stance from birth, reflecting incomplete cerebellar development due to viral interference during a critical window of fetal neurological development.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Complete anencephaly in every case overstates the typical defect; cerebellar hypoplasia specifically, not universal absence of the brain, is the classic finding.
  • Universal deafness with no other signs does not match the documented neurological presentation.
  • Polymelia (extra limbs) is not the documented congenital defect associated with BVDV.
Know More
  • Eye defects and skeletal deformities can also occur with mid-gestation fetal BVDV infection.
  • Timing of infection during gestation strongly influences the specific outcome.
  • Affected calves with cerebellar hypoplasia may survive but show lifelong incoordination.
  • Vaccination timed appropriately before breeding helps reduce the risk of these fetal outcomes.

posts.post_title: Bulk milk PCR testing application in BVD control
posts.post_content: Bulk milk PCR testing is a useful surveillance tool in BVD control programs primarily because it can do what?

_aimcq_options.text: Screen an entire dairy herd's milk supply for evidence of BVDV circulation
Replace the need for any individual animal testing forever

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Screen an entire dairy herd's milk supply for evidence of BVDV circulation

Bulk milk PCR testing allows efficient herd-level screening for evidence of BVDV circulation.

Correct Option Explanation

This cost-effective surveillance approach can flag herds warranting further individual animal testing to identify and remove specific persistently infected animals, without needing to test every individual cow upfront.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • PCR testing is diagnostic, not therapeutic; it cannot cure persistently infected animals.
  • A positive bulk milk result typically prompts further individual testing, so it does not replace individual testing altogether.
  • Bulk milk PCR for BVD specifically targets BVDV nucleic acid, not unrelated bacterial mastitis pathogens.
Know More
  • Newborn calves are commonly individually tested (ear-notch) before entering a herd.
  • National BVD eradication programs often combine bulk milk screening with targeted individual testing.
  • Several European countries have successfully achieved national BVD-free status using such combined approaches.
  • Biosecurity measures help prevent reintroduction of BVDV into BVD-free herds.

posts.post_title: Severity comparison between BVDV genotypes
posts.post_content: Compared to BVDV-1, certain BVDV-2 strains are particularly notable for being associated with what?

_aimcq_options.text: Complete inability to cause persistent infection
Exclusive infection of poultry, not cattle
Total lack of any cytopathic biotype

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: More severe acute disease outbreaks

Certain BVDV-2 strains are notable for causing more severe acute disease outbreaks compared to typical BVDV-1 infections.

Correct Option Explanation

These severe outbreaks can include high fever, profound thrombocytopenia, and increased mortality, prompting the inclusion of BVDV-2 antigens in many modern combination vaccines to ensure broader protection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • BVDV-2, like BVDV-1, is fully capable of causing persistent infection via the non-cytopathic biotype.
  • BVDV-2 infects cattle (and other ruminants), not poultry; it is not a poultry pathogen.
  • BVDV-2 strains, like BVDV-1, can occur as either cytopathic or non-cytopathic biotypes.
Know More
  • Modern combination vaccines often include antigens from both BVDV-1 and BVDV-2 for broader protection.
  • Severe BVDV-2 outbreaks in North America in the 1990s highlighted the clinical importance of this genotype.
  • Accurate genotyping helps guide vaccine selection and outbreak investigation.
  • Both genotypes contribute to the overall economic burden of BVD in cattle industries worldwide.

posts.post_title: Bluetongue virus outer capsid protein determining serotype
posts.post_content: Which bluetongue virus protein primarily determines the serotype of a given strain, and is a key target for serotype-specific diagnostic tests?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: VP2

VP2, the main outer capsid protein, is the primary serotype-determining protein of bluetongue virus.

Correct Option Explanation

Because VP2 varies significantly between the 24-27 recognised serotypes, it is a key target for serotype-specific serological and molecular diagnostic tests, and for guiding vaccine strain selection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Haemagglutinin (H) is a paramyxovirus (e.g. rinderpest, CDV) protein, not a bluetongue virus protein.
  • Matrix protein (M) and fusion protein (F) are proteins characteristic of enveloped viruses like paramyxoviruses, not the non-enveloped orbivirus bluetongue virus.
Know More
  • Bluetongue virus has 10 dsRNA genome segments encoding various structural and non-structural proteins.
  • Group-specific antigens (like VP7) are used in broader serogroup diagnostic tests (e.g. AGID).
  • Reassortment between different bluetongue virus serotypes can occur when a host is co-infected.
  • Serotype-specific vaccination is necessary because of limited cross-protection between serotypes.

posts.post_title: Reproductive impact of bluetongue virus infection
posts.post_content: Besides direct clinical signs like tongue cyanosis and coronitis, bluetongue virus infection in pregnant ewes can also cause what reproductive consequence?

_aimcq_options.text: Abortion and congenital defects in lambs
Guaranteed twin births in every pregnancy
Permanent, universal infertility in all exposed ewes

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Abortion and congenital defects in lambs

Bluetongue virus infection during pregnancy can cause abortion and congenital defects in lambs.

Correct Option Explanation

This reproductive impact adds to the overall economic burden of the disease beyond the direct clinical illness in adult sheep, similar in concept to reproductive losses seen with other pestiviruses and orbiviruses affecting livestock.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Guaranteed twin births is unrelated to and not a documented consequence of bluetongue infection.
  • Permanent, universal infertility in every exposed ewe overstates the documented reproductive impact.
  • 'No reproductive effects whatsoever' contradicts the well-documented abortion and congenital defect risk.
Know More
  • Timing of infection during gestation influences the specific reproductive outcome.
  • Vaccination programs aim to protect breeding ewes before or during early pregnancy in endemic regions.
  • Surveillance of reproductive losses can sometimes be an early indicator of bluetongue virus circulation.
  • Vector control remains an important complementary strategy alongside vaccination.

posts.post_title: Genome segment count shared by AHS and bluetongue viruses
posts.post_content: Like bluetongue virus, African horse sickness virus has how many double-stranded RNA genome segments?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Ten

African horse sickness virus has ten double-stranded RNA genome segments, matching the genome structure of related orbiviruses like bluetongue virus.

Correct Option Explanation

This shared genome architecture reflects their common family, Reoviridae, and genus, Orbivirus, though AHSV and bluetongue virus remain distinct in host range and serotype composition.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Two and five undercount the documented segment number for this genus.
  • Twenty overcounts the documented segment number.
Know More
  • Segmented genomes allow for genetic reassortment between different strains during co-infection.
  • Each segment encodes specific structural or non-structural proteins.
  • Molecular diagnostics like RT-PCR target conserved regions of these segments.
  • Understanding genome structure aids in vaccine and diagnostic test development.

posts.post_title: Type of vaccine used against African horse sickness in endemic regions
posts.post_content: In regions where African horse sickness is endemic, control commonly relies on which type of vaccine?

_aimcq_options.text: A single-dose mRNA vaccine used since the 1960s
No vaccine of any kind is ever used

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Live attenuated, polyvalent vaccine

A live attenuated, polyvalent vaccine, covering multiple serotypes, is commonly used in AHS-endemic regions.

Correct Option Explanation

Given the nine recognised serotypes of AHSV, polyvalent formulations help provide broader protection, though careful vaccine strain selection and administration protocols are needed to manage the complexity of multiple live strains.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • mRNA vaccine technology is a much more recent development and was not the traditional AHS vaccine platform used since the 1960s.
  • Antibiotics have no effect against this viral disease.
  • Vaccination is, in fact, actively used in endemic areas, contradicting 'no vaccine of any kind'.
Know More
  • Vaccination is combined with vector control and movement restrictions for comprehensive AHS management.
  • Newly developed vaccine technologies are being explored to improve safety and efficacy.
  • Countries free of AHS maintain strict import restrictions on horses from endemic zones.
  • Rapid diagnosis and reporting are essential given the severity of the disease.

posts.post_title: Mixed clinical form of African horse sickness
posts.post_content: Besides the peracute (pulmonary) and subacute (cardiac) forms, African horse sickness can also present as which additional clinical form?

_aimcq_options.text: A mixed form combining pulmonary and cardiac features
A purely dermatological form with no internal organ involvement
A form exclusive to newborn foals only
A form that only affects the reproductive tract

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A mixed form combining pulmonary and cardiac features

A mixed form, combining features of both the pulmonary and cardiac presentations, also occurs in African horse sickness.

Correct Option Explanation

This form illustrates the systemic nature of the disease, since severe orbivirus infection can simultaneously damage the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, contributing to the overall high case fatality seen with virulent strains.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A purely dermatological form with no internal organ involvement is not among the documented clinical forms of AHS.
  • AHS is not restricted to newborn foals; horses of various ages are susceptible.
  • AHS is not documented as a reproductive-tract-exclusive disease form.
Know More
  • A milder 'horse sickness fever' form can also occur, particularly in more resistant equid species.
  • Clinical presentation severity often correlates with the equid species affected (horses being most susceptible).
  • Diagnosis relies on combining clinical signs with laboratory confirmation, given overlapping presentations between forms.
  • Prompt veterinary attention improves the chance of survival in less severe presentations.

posts.post_title: Bursal lesion progression pattern in infectious bursal disease
posts.post_content: Following infection with IBDV, the bursa of Fabricius typically shows an initial swelling and haemorrhage phase followed by what later change?

_aimcq_options.text: Permanent, progressive bursal enlargement with no regression ever
Complete replacement of the bursa with bone tissue
No change at all after the initial swelling

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bursal atrophy

After the initial swelling and haemorrhagic phase, the bursa typically undergoes atrophy (shrinkage).

Correct Option Explanation

This progression from acute inflammation to lymphoid depletion and atrophy reflects the destructive impact of the virus on bursal B-lymphocyte populations, underlying the resulting immunosuppression in survivors.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Permanent, progressive enlargement with no regression contradicts the well-documented atrophic endpoint of bursal pathology.
  • Replacement with bone tissue is not a documented pathological change in this disease.
  • Significant further change does occur, namely atrophy, so 'no change at all' is incorrect.
Know More
  • Histopathology shows lymphocyte depletion and necrosis within bursal follicles.
  • Bursal atrophy correlates with the degree of resulting immunosuppression.
  • Very virulent IBDV strains (vvIBDV) can cause particularly severe bursal damage and high mortality.
  • Vaccination timing is carefully managed to protect the bursa before peak susceptibility age.

posts.post_title: Consequence of immunosuppression from infectious bursal disease
posts.post_content: Chickens that survive infectious bursal disease with significant bursal damage often show what important downstream consequence?

_aimcq_options.text: Reduced responsiveness to other vaccines and increased susceptibility to secondary infections
Permanent immunity to every other poultry disease
Enhanced egg production for the rest of their lives
No measurable effect on their immune function

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Reduced responsiveness to other vaccines and increased susceptibility to secondary infections

Bursal damage leads to reduced vaccine responsiveness and increased susceptibility to secondary infections.

Correct Option Explanation

Because the bursa of Fabricius is essential for normal B-lymphocyte development, its destruction compromises the bird's ability to mount effective antibody responses, including to subsequent vaccinations against unrelated pathogens.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bursal damage impairs, rather than confers, broad immunity to other diseases.
  • Enhanced egg production is not a documented consequence of this immunosuppressive disease.
  • The immunosuppressive effect is well documented and clinically significant, contradicting 'no measurable effect'.
Know More
  • Secondary bacterial and viral infections are more common and more severe in immunosuppressed flocks.
  • Vaccine failures against other poultry diseases can be linked back to underlying IBDV-induced immunosuppression.
  • Bio-secure hatchery practices and appropriately timed vaccination help minimise this impact.
  • Ongoing research into genetic resistance aims to reduce the industry-wide burden of this disease.

posts.post_title: Timing challenge for infectious bursal disease vaccination
posts.post_content: Vaccination programs against infectious bursal disease must be carefully timed to account for what interfering factor in young chicks?

_aimcq_options.text: Maternally-derived antibody, which can neutralise live vaccine virus if given too early
The chick's body temperature, which is irrelevant to vaccine timing
The colour of the chick's feathers
The time of day the vaccine is administered

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Maternally-derived antibody, which can neutralise live vaccine virus if given too early

Maternally-derived antibody can neutralise live vaccine virus if vaccination is given too early, reducing vaccine efficacy.

Correct Option Explanation

Because maternal antibody levels vary between chicks and decline over time, vaccination programs often use monitoring (e.g. ELISA titre testing) or intermediate-plus vaccine strains to determine optimal vaccination timing for a given flock.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Body temperature is not the key interfering factor discussed for IBD vaccine timing in this material.
  • Feather colour has no bearing on vaccine timing or efficacy.
  • Time of day of administration is not the documented critical timing factor for this vaccine.
Know More
  • Breeder flock vaccination boosts maternal antibody levels passed to chicks via the egg yolk.
  • Intermediate and intermediate-plus vaccine strains are designed to break through varying levels of maternal antibody.
  • In ovo vaccination technology is used for some IBD vaccines, administered during incubation.
  • Regular serological monitoring helps optimise flock-specific vaccination schedules.

posts.post_title: Subfamily classification shared by pseudorabies and Marek's disease viruses
posts.post_content: Pseudorabies virus and Marek's disease virus are both classified within which subfamily of Herpesviridae?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Alphaherpesvirinae

Both pseudorabies virus and Marek's disease virus belong to subfamily Alphaherpesvirinae.

Correct Option Explanation

Alphaherpesviruses are generally characterised by a relatively short reproductive cycle, rapid cell-to-cell spread, and the ability to establish latency in sensory ganglia (though Marek's disease virus is notable for also being oncogenic).

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Betaherpesvirinae includes cytomegaloviruses, characterised by a longer reproductive cycle, not the subfamily of these two viruses.
  • Gammaherpesvirinae includes lymphotropic herpesviruses with different latency patterns (often in lymphoid tissue), not this subfamily.
  • 'Deltaherpesvirinae' is not a recognised standard herpesvirus subfamily.
Know More
  • Alphaherpesviruses typically cause more acute, cytolytic disease compared to some other subfamilies.
  • Latency in sensory ganglia allows for periodic reactivation and shedding under stress.
  • Marek's disease virus is unusual among alphaherpesviruses for its strong oncogenic potential.
  • Understanding subfamily characteristics helps guide vaccine and diagnostic strategy development.

posts.post_title: Purpose of gene-deleted marker vaccines in pseudorabies control
posts.post_content: Gene-deleted 'marker' vaccines used in pseudorabies (Aujeszky's disease) eradication programs primarily allow for what?

_aimcq_options.text: Differentiation of vaccinated from naturally infected pigs (DIVA strategy)
Complete elimination of the need for any serological testing
Guaranteed sterilising immunity that prevents all future infection
Use exclusively in cattle rather than pigs

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Differentiation of vaccinated from naturally infected pigs (DIVA strategy)

Gene-deleted marker vaccines enable the DIVA (Differentiating Infected from Vaccinated Animals) strategy.

Correct Option Explanation

By deleting a specific viral gene (commonly gE) from the vaccine strain, serological tests can distinguish antibodies from vaccination (lacking anti-gE antibody) from those due to natural infection (with anti-gE antibody present), supporting targeted eradication efforts.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • DIVA strategy specifically relies on continued, targeted serological testing, not its elimination.
  • No vaccine guarantees complete sterilising immunity; marker vaccines primarily aid surveillance and reduce clinical disease and shedding.
  • These marker vaccines were developed and are used specifically in pigs, the natural host for pseudorabies virus, not primarily in cattle.
Know More
  • DIVA strategies have been successfully applied in several national Aujeszky's disease eradication programs.
  • Combining marker vaccination with targeted culling of seropositive (gE-positive) pigs accelerates eradication.
  • Many developed pig-producing countries have achieved commercial herd freedom from pseudorabies using this approach.
  • Ongoing surveillance remains important to detect and respond to any reintroduction.

posts.post_title: Genome type of African swine fever virus
posts.post_content: African swine fever virus has which type of genome, distinguishing it from most other important veterinary viruses covered in this course?

_aimcq_options.text: A single, large, linear double-stranded DNA genome
A segmented, single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: A single, large, linear double-stranded DNA genome

ASFV has a single, large, linear double-stranded DNA genome, one of the largest among animal DNA viruses.

Correct Option Explanation

This DNA genome, combined with its arthropod-borne (tick vector) transmission, makes ASFV taxonomically and biologically unique compared to most other viruses covered in veterinary virology, most of which are RNA viruses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A segmented, single-stranded positive-sense RNA genome describes viruses like influenza A (in the segmented sense) or picornaviruses (in the positive-sense RNA sense), not ASFV's DNA genome.
  • A segmented, double-stranded RNA genome describes viruses like bluetongue virus (Reoviridae), not ASFV.
  • A non-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome describes viruses like rabies virus, not ASFV.
Know More
  • ASFV encodes numerous proteins that help it evade the host's immune response.
  • Its large genome size supports a complex replication and immune evasion strategy within host cells.
  • The DNA genome allows for relatively stable genetic identity compared to many rapidly mutating RNA viruses, though genetic diversity among global strains still exists.
  • Understanding genome biology supports ongoing vaccine development efforts.

posts.post_title: Zoonotic potential of African swine fever
posts.post_content: Does African swine fever virus pose a direct zoonotic risk to humans?

_aimcq_options.text: No, ASF has no zoonotic potential and does not infect humans
Yes, it causes a mild rash in nearly all exposed humans
Yes, it is a leading cause of human encephalitis worldwide
Yes, it causes severe respiratory failure in most exposed people

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: No, ASF has no zoonotic potential and does not infect humans

African swine fever has no zoonotic potential; it does not infect humans.

Correct Option Explanation

Despite its severe impact on pig populations and the resulting economic consequences, ASF is exclusively a disease of suids (domestic pigs and wild boar/warthogs), posing no direct health threat to people handling infected animals or products.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • ASF does not cause any rash or disease in humans, contrary to this option.
  • ASF is not linked to human encephalitis; it is not documented to infect humans at all.
  • ASF does not cause respiratory or any other disease in humans, contrary to this option.
Know More
  • Despite lacking zoonotic risk, ASF remains one of the most economically devastating swine diseases globally due to its high mortality and trade impact.
  • Strict import controls on pork products help prevent international spread of the virus itself, unrelated to any human health risk.
  • Public communication during outbreaks often needs to clarify this lack of human health risk to avoid unnecessary panic.
  • Resources during outbreaks are focused on animal health, biosecurity, and economic mitigation rather than any human medical response.

posts.post_title: Reason iatrogenic transmission is a concern for equine infectious anaemia
posts.post_content: Besides biting flies, equine infectious anaemia virus can also spread iatrogenically through what practice if proper precautions are not taken?

_aimcq_options.text: Use of contaminated needles or surgical instruments between horses
Feeding horses hay from a different farm
Grooming horses with a clean, dedicated brush per horse
Routine hoof trimming with properly disinfected tools

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Use of contaminated needles or surgical instruments between horses

Contaminated needles or surgical instruments used between horses can iatrogenically transmit EIAV.

Correct Option Explanation

Because the virus is blood-borne, any practice that transfers even small amounts of blood between horses on shared, unsterilised equipment carries a transmission risk, making single-use needles and proper instrument sterilisation important preventive measures.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Feeding hay from a different farm is not a documented blood-borne transmission route for EIAV.
  • Grooming with a clean, dedicated brush per horse is a preventive practice, not a transmission risk.
  • Hoof trimming with properly disinfected tools is a preventive practice, not a described transmission risk, provided proper disinfection is maintained.
Know More
  • Good veterinary and farm hygiene practices, including single-use needles, help reduce iatrogenic spread risk.
  • Fly control measures address the primary natural transmission route.
  • Regular Coggins testing helps identify infected horses before they can serve as a source for further spread.
  • Strict biosecurity is especially important in high-density equine facilities like breeding farms and racetracks.

posts.post_title: Effect of infectious bronchitis vaccination timing on reproductive tract protection
posts.post_content: To help minimise permanent oviduct damage from infectious bronchitis virus, vaccination is generally most important during which period of a pullet's life?

_aimcq_options.text: Before the onset of lay, while the reproductive tract is still developing
Only after the bird has already been laying eggs for over a year
Vaccination timing has no bearing on reproductive tract outcomes
Only during the last week before slaughter

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Before the onset of lay, while the reproductive tract is still developing

Vaccination before the onset of lay, while the reproductive tract is still developing, is most important for minimising permanent oviduct damage.

Correct Option Explanation

Since infection of very young pullets can permanently damage the developing oviduct (leading to 'false layers'), establishing protective immunity before this vulnerable developmental window is a key goal of layer flock vaccination programs.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Vaccinating only after a year of laying misses the critical early developmental window when damage is most likely to become permanent.
  • Timing does, in fact, significantly affect reproductive tract outcomes, contradicting 'no bearing'.
  • Vaccination just before slaughter would not address reproductive tract protection relevant to a laying flock's productive life.
Know More
  • Multiple vaccinations, often combining live and inactivated types, are used across a layer flock's rearing period.
  • Serotype diversity requires selecting vaccine strains relevant to the region's circulating IBV strains.
  • Good biosecurity reduces the risk of early-life exposure before vaccine-induced immunity is established.
  • Egg production monitoring can serve as an early indicator of a possible IBV outbreak in a flock.

posts.post_title: Species targeted by transmissible gastroenteritis versus infectious bronchitis viruses
posts.post_content: Transmissible gastroenteritis virus and infectious bronchitis virus, though both coronaviruses, differ in that they are natural pathogens of which respective host species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Pigs (TGE) and chickens (IB)

TGE virus is a pathogen of pigs, while infectious bronchitis virus is a pathogen of chickens.

Correct Option Explanation

Although both belong to family Coronaviridae, they occupy very different genera and host niches, illustrating how coronaviruses have diversified to infect a wide range of host species with distinct clinical presentations.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Horses and cattle are not the documented natural hosts for TGE and IB viruses respectively in this material.
  • Cats and dogs are affected by other coronaviruses (e.g. feline infectious peritonitis virus, canine coronavirus), not TGE or IB virus specifically.
  • Sheep and goats are not the documented hosts for TGE or IB viruses.
Know More
  • TGE virus mainly affects the intestinal tract of young piglets.
  • IB virus mainly affects the respiratory tract, kidneys, and reproductive tract of chickens.
  • Porcine respiratory coronavirus (PRCV) is a related deletion mutant of TGE virus with altered tropism.
  • Species specificity generally limits cross-species transmission between these particular coronaviruses.

posts.post_title: Effect of good farm hygiene on transmissible gastroenteritis persistence
posts.post_content: All-in/all-out management and thorough cleaning between pig batches help control transmissible gastroenteritis primarily by achieving what?

_aimcq_options.text: Breaking the chain of transmission between successive groups of pigs
Curing pigs that are already clinically affected
Eliminating the need for maternal antibody protection entirely
Providing a permanent, lifelong vaccine effect

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Breaking the chain of transmission between successive groups of pigs

These management practices help break the chain of transmission between successive groups of pigs on a farm.

Correct Option Explanation

By thoroughly cleaning and allowing downtime between batches, residual virus in the environment is reduced or eliminated before a new, naive group of piglets arrives, lowering the risk of new outbreaks.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • These management practices are preventive, not therapeutic; they do not cure pigs that are already clinically affected.
  • Maternal (lactogenic) antibody protection remains important for young piglets regardless of these hygiene measures; they are complementary, not substitutes.
  • These are management practices, not a vaccine, and do not confer any lasting immunological protection themselves.
Know More
  • TGE virus can persist in the environment for a limited but significant period, making cleaning protocols important.
  • Combining good hygiene with sow vaccination programs offers the most effective overall control strategy.
  • Rapid diagnosis of new cases helps limit further spread within a facility.
  • Biosecurity between different age groups and units further reduces cross-contamination risk on a farm.

posts.post_title: General principle linking virus family to disease severity across this course
posts.post_content: Across the diseases covered in this course, which general principle most consistently helps explain why some viral infections (e.g. rabies, ASF) are almost universally fatal while others (e.g. mild strains of avian influenza) are often self-limiting?

_aimcq_options.text: Virulence varies with the specific virus strain, its tissue tropism, and host immune response
All viruses within a single family always cause identical disease severity
Only DNA viruses can ever cause severe or fatal disease
Disease severity is determined solely by the animal's breed, with no role for the virus itself

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Virulence varies with the specific virus strain, its tissue tropism, and host immune response

Virulence depends on the specific strain, its tissue tropism, and the host's immune response, rather than family membership alone.

Correct Option Explanation

This course illustrates this principle repeatedly: NDV pathotypes range from lentogenic to velogenic, BVDV and CSFV have cytopathic/non-cytopathic biotypes with different consequences, and AI strains range from low to highly pathogenic — all within single virus species or families.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Virus families in this course show substantial internal variation in virulence (e.g. NDV pathotypes, AI pathotypes), contradicting uniform severity within a family.
  • Both RNA viruses (e.g. rabies, a negative-sense RNA virus) and DNA viruses (e.g. ASFV) can cause severe or fatal disease, so genome type alone does not determine severity.
  • While host factors like breed and age can influence outcomes, the specific virus strain and its properties play a central, well-documented role, not host factors alone.
Know More
  • Molecular markers (e.g. F protein cleavage site in NDV) help predict virulence in some viruses.
  • Understanding these virulence determinants supports rational vaccine and diagnostic test design.
  • Ongoing surveillance for emerging virulent strains remains an important part of veterinary disease control.
  • A 'one size fits all' view of viral virulence oversimplifies the complex biology covered throughout this course.

posts.post_title: Common theme in modern control strategies across major veterinary viral diseases
posts.post_content: Across most of the major viral diseases covered in this course, effective long-term control typically relies on a combination of which approaches?

_aimcq_options.text: Vaccination, biosecurity/movement control, and surveillance/diagnostic testing
Antibiotic therapy alone, with no other measures needed
Complete reliance on natural herd immunity with no intervention
Dietary supplementation as the sole control measure

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Vaccination, biosecurity/movement control, and surveillance/diagnostic testing

Effective control typically combines vaccination, biosecurity and movement control, and ongoing surveillance/diagnostic testing.

Correct Option Explanation

This integrated approach appears repeatedly throughout the course, from ND and FMD vaccination programs, to BVD/CSF test-and-cull strategies, to AHS and bluetongue vector control combined with vaccination, reflecting that no single tool alone is sufficient for most of these diseases.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Antibiotics are ineffective against viral pathogens and cannot substitute for these integrated control measures.
  • Relying solely on natural herd immunity, without vaccination or biosecurity, generally allows for prolonged, costly outbreaks as seen historically with several diseases in this course.
  • Dietary supplementation alone does not address the underlying viral transmission and immunity issues central to these diseases.
Know More
  • Successful eradication programs, like that for rinderpest, exemplify this integrated, multi-pronged approach.
  • Emerging diagnostic technologies (PCR, ELISA) increasingly support faster, more targeted control decisions.
  • International cooperation and reporting (e.g. via OIE) support coordinated global responses to major outbreaks.
  • Ongoing research into new vaccine platforms continues to improve options for previously hard-to-control diseases like ASF.
